body.p: On 30 October 2026 HSE published the outcome of a prosecution following a fire on 26 July 2024 at the Old Telephone Exchange development in Staines-upon-Thames. Four subcontractors working under the control of C Watkins Plumbing Limited were installing an air source heat pump on the roof of a 14-storey apartment building under construction. Sparks from welding ignited uncovered rigid foam insulation laid across the roof. The fire developed quickly, spread across the roof space and burned until the fuel was exhausted. The workers escaped through a single opening in the floor and down a ladder to Level 14. There was no other way off the roof, no means of raising the alarm and no fire extinguishers present.

The investigation found that the company failed to plan, manage and monitor the hot works. Although the company had policies that required them, no risk assessment or method statement was in place and no permit to work was issued for the welding. The company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 15(2) of the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 and was fined £20,000 with £8,270 costs at Staines Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026. Temporary roof access and the hot-works activity on that access are both temporary works / high-risk activities that sit inside the project temporary works procedure and the CDM duties to plan, manage and monitor. A single escape route and absent fire controls turn an otherwise routine welding task into a foreseeable life-safety failure.

ul: Treat temporary roof access (scaffold, ladder, platform or other arrangement) as a temporary works item requiring a design brief, entry on the live Temporary Works Register and acceptance under the project procedure before use.
Identify combustible materials (insulation, packaging, temporary coverings) on or adjacent to the working surface as part of the design brief and risk assessment for hot works.
Require a task-specific risk assessment and method statement for hot works that addresses ignition sources, fuel, escape routes, means of raising the alarm and extinguishing arrangements.
Issue a hot-works permit only after the temporary access has been inspected, the escape route(s) verified, fire extinguishers provided and a competent person has confirmed the controls.

Confirm that the temporary access itself has more than one means of escape where reasonably practicable, or that residual single-route risk is formally accepted with additional controls under the project procedure.
Link the permit-to-work to the temporary works permit-to-load / permit-to-use so that hot works cannot proceed on an unaccepted or uninspected temporary structure.
Review fire safety arrangements against HSG168 Fire safety in construction and keep them under review as the temporary condition changes.

body.p: Build UK published Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard on 1 November 2026. The Building Safety section (Section 7) now operates on an active opt-out basis. Scaffolding and temporary works are not within the scope of the Building Regulations that regulate ‘building work’, unless they form part of the structure once complete. Companies that do not undertake regulated building work must opt out of Section 7 and provide a statement confirming that they do not carry out work covered by the Building Regulations. Competence-related questions previously located in Section 7 have been moved to the Quality section (Section 5) so that they are completed by all companies. Additional items, including a drugs and alcohol policy and fraud prevention procedures, are now mandatory for every company.

The clarification removes questions that were not applicable to pure temporary works or scaffolding activity and that had created difficulty during pre-qualification. It does not reduce the requirement to demonstrate organisational capability, competence or safety and quality management. Temporary works remain subject to the project temporary works procedure under BS 5975-1:2024 and to the duties in CDM 2015. Pre-qualification evidence and the live control of design, installation, inspection and striking on site are separate. Principal contractors and clients who use the Common Assessment Standard will still expect evidence of competence and controlled temporary works processes.

ul: Confirm with your Recognised Assessment Body whether Version 6 applies to your next certification and prepare the required opt-out statement if you do not undertake building work regulated by the Building Regulations.
Ensure competence evidence that has moved to the Quality section remains current and can be produced on request.
Keep the project temporary works procedure, Temporary Works Register, design briefs, category checks and permits independent of pre-qualification status.
Do not treat an opt-out from Section 7 as a reduction in the need for design, checking or competent supervision of temporary works on site.
Where temporary works later form part of the permanent structure, reassess whether the Building Safety section applies and record the decision.
Update supply-chain and pre-qualification files so that clients and principal contractors can see both the CAS position and the temporary works control arrangements.

posts.title: No design, incomplete load path, ongoing investigation: temporary works control still matters
posts.excerpt: June 2026 HSE fines followed a City of London temporary platform collapse with no design or safe-load calculation. CROSS-UK Report 1539 (May 2026) records propping issued without verifying the existing structure could carry redistributed loads. An HSE investigation continues after the 21 October 2026 Banbury scaffolding and building partial collapse. Contractors must keep temporary structures inside the BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM process: design brief, verified load path, register, permit and competent supervision.
posts.linkedinReady:
Temporary wooden platforms that collect concrete debris still need a design and a safe working load.

In June 2026 the Health and Safety Executive reported that two companies were fined after a temporary platform collapsed during floor cutting in the City of London, fracturing a worker’s neck and back. The investigation found no design for the platforms and no calculation of safe loading. The person completing the inspection form was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear debris were not enough without a defined load limit and monitoring.

CROSS-UK Report 1539 (published May 2026) shows a parallel gap in propping. Heavy-duty props were issued for column replacement, but the designer had not checked whether the existing beams and slab could transfer the redistributed loads. Once opened up, the beams and slab were shown to be inadequate in bending and shear. Without further temporary works the building could have partially collapsed.

An ongoing HSE investigation follows the partial collapse of scaffolding and an apartment block under construction in Banbury on 21 October 2026. Two of nine workers were hospitalised. Details of cause remain under enquiry; the practical reminder is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems must stay within the project temporary works procedure.

BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 require a controlled process: design brief, competent design and check, live register, permit to load, and competent supervision. Temporary structures are not “just timber” or “just props.” They carry foreseeable loads and must have a verified load path from the point of application to a suitable foundation or support.

Identify the temporary condition. Design or confirm a standard solution within its limits. Check it. Permit it. Inspect it. Strike it under control.

body.p: On 15 June 2026 HSE published the outcome of prosecutions against Roots Contractors Limited and Diacutt Limited following a February 2024 incident at Paxton House, City of London. Temporary wooden platforms built to collect concrete cores and debris collapsed onto a drilling operative working below, causing fractures to the neck and back and a brain bleed. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe level of loading. An inspection form was completed by a person who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear platforms existed, but no safe load was known and clearing was not monitored. Planning, supervision and coordination of the drilling work were also deficient.

CROSS-UK Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, describes temporary works for replacement of a defective reinforced concrete column in a multi-storey block of flats. Heavy-duty props had already been installed and a drawing issued. The props themselves were capable of the required forces, but no evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up showed that the existing beams and slab were not strong enough to transfer the redistributed loads and would fail in bending and shear. The Reporter designed additional temporary works and a method statement. Without those measures a significant part of the building could have collapsed. The Expert Panel noted the need for a verified load path from the point of application through to a suitable support, and for the temporary works procedure (including TWC and checking) to be applied.

On 21 October 2026 scaffolding and an apartment block under construction partially collapsed in Cherwell Street, Banbury. Nine workers were on site; two were taken to hospital. HSE is investigating. Oxfordshire County Council partially reopened the road on 30 October after safety advice, with further temporary closures expected for crane operations to make the site safe. No confirmed cause has been published; the reminder for contractors is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems remain subject to the project temporary works procedure while the investigation continues.

ul: Treat any temporary platform, crash deck, propping system or scaffold as a temporary works item requiring entry on the live Temporary Works Register.
Issue a design brief that defines foreseeable loads, including debris accumulation, and confirm either a project-specific design or a standard solution used strictly within its stated limits.
When propping or supporting an existing structure, require verification of the full load path, including capacity of beams, slabs, walls and foundations that will receive redistributed loads.
Ensure the person completing inspections or issuing permits is a competent Temporary Works Coordinator or Supervisor under the project procedure.
Do not load, alter or strike temporary works until a formal permit has been issued after the required checks.
Maintain documented supervision and clear communication so that workers are not placed under unauthorised or overloaded temporary structures.
Close the register entry only after verification, acceptance and controlled striking under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1613, published on 28 October 2026, records a chartered structural engineer’s report of multiple unauthorised changes during construction of an industrial building extension. Construction had commenced without planning approval, without a Building Regulations application, and without compliance with CDM. After a site inspection the Reporter identified numerous departures from the original design that had been implemented without consultation or design review. A steel grillage platform carrying approximately 5 tonnes of plant had been installed although it was not in the original design brief; the structure was erected before any design verification. The main steel frame had not accounted for the additional plant load. Subsequent checks showed that additional bracing was required to some posts. Other defects included alteration of gable frames to portal frames without review, an undesigned beam supporting a windpost, modified windpost head connections that transferred roof loads, bracing interrupted at a splice (leading to overstressed columns), undesigned column and windpost splices, omission of lower-level bracing for openings, uniform pad foundations with no evidence of design (inadequate for uplift in braced bays), and a retaining wall constructed without prior design.

Additional plant platforms, temporary stability bracing, load-path changes and undesigned connections are temporary works items or design-risk items under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015. Erecting them before verification places the load path outside the controlled design. The Expert Panel states that the number and extent of the changes are a significant cause for concern and that unauthorised alterations create a risk that safety-critical decisions are made without appropriate technical scrutiny. Where a contractor or others alter a design without obtaining approval from the original designer, they assume responsibility for those changes and the associated risks. Effective management of design changes relies on all dutyholders discharging their responsibilities under CDM 2015, including coordination of design and management of design risk. Seemingly minor changes can have significant implications for structural performance and temporary stability.

ul: Treat any additional plant support platform, grillage, temporary bracing or undesigned connection as a temporary works item requiring entry on the Temporary Works Register.
Issue a design brief before erection. Do not allow the platform or altered framing to be constructed until the design (or confirmed standard solution), category check and permit-to-load are in place.
Confirm that the primary structure has been designed or checked for the additional loads and any change in load path or stability system.
Require formal design-change control: proposed changes must be reviewed and accepted by the responsible designer (or temporary works designer) before implementation.
Where design responsibilities are split, establish clear overall coordination so that the completed structure (permanent plus temporary) functions safely as a whole.
Use site inspections by a competent person (TWC or TWS) to identify departures from the approved design before they become embedded.
Record the residual risks and any remedial works required, and close the temporary works item only after verification and acceptance under the project procedure.

body.p: Build UK has confirmed that Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard takes effect on 1 November 2026. Scaffolding and temporary works contractors whose activities are not covered by the Building Regulations must actively opt out of Section 7 (Building Safety) and provide a statement confirming they do not undertake work covered by those regulations. The change follows NASC correspondence with MHCLG and subsequent clarification from the Housing Minister to the Building Safety Regulator that scaffolding and temporary works are not generally within the Building Regulations governing building work unless they form part of the completed structure.

CAS is widely used by principal contractors and clients to assess supply-chain organisational capability. posts.title: Scaffold dismantling: exclusion zone and controlled lowering failed — a fatal board fall
posts.excerpt: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after pleading guilty to a breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. Samuel Magill, a 60-year-old collection driver, was struck on the head by a 2.4 m metal scaffold board that fell approximately 8 m during dismantling on Lisburn Road, Belfast, on 18 December 2024. He died on 5 February 2025. HSENI found the company had not adequately managed the exclusion zone so that people not directly involved in the dismantling could approach the scaffold. He was struck at the outer edge of the zone next to the pavement. The case underlines that dismantling is a temporary works activity requiring controlled lowering and enforced exclusion of non-essential personnel.

body.p: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after pleading guilty to a single breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. Samuel Magill, aged 60 and employed as a collection driver, was collecting scaffold components from a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, on 18 December 2024. During dismantling, a metal scaffold board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the works, fell around 8 m, and struck him on the head. He was taken to hospital and died on 5 February 2025. He had parked on the pavement outside the site and was struck at the extremity of the exclusion zone adjacent to the pavement.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone during the dismantling phase. Measures were inadequate to prevent people who were not directly involved in the dismantling from approaching the scaffold. Inspector Kevin Campbell described the incident as entirely preventable and emphasised that employers must have robust procedures to ensure equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, and that exclusion zones must be clearly identified with measures to prevent unauthorised entry. Scaffold dismantling is temporary works. The load path changes as members are removed; falling objects and people outside the working gang (including collection drivers, site staff and the public) create a high-consequence interface. Standard does not automatically mean low risk.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Treat the dismantling sequence as a temporary works activity requiring design or standard-solution verification under the project temporary works procedure (BS 5975-1:2024 management framework).
Define the method of controlled lowering in the method statement and RAMS. Do not rely on free-fall or uncontrolled release of boards, tubes or fittings.
Set the exclusion zone size and boundaries on the basis of the height of work, the components being handled, and the likelihood of dislodgement. Mark it clearly and enforce it.
Control the interface with collection, delivery or other vehicles. Parking and pedestrian approaches must not place people inside or at the edge of the zone.
Use a permit-to-dismantle / permit-to-strike (or equivalent hold point) that confirms the sequence, exclusion zone, supervision and competence before work starts.
Ensure the TWS or competent supervisor is present and that non-essential personnel are kept clear until the zone is released.
Record the activity on the Temporary Works Register and close it only after the scaffold is fully struck and the area is safe.

body.p: Storm Austen produced an official UK peak gust of 76 mph on 23 October 2026. The Met Office recorded 76 mph at St Mary’s Airport on the Isles of Scilly, 75 mph at the Isle of Portland and Needles Old Battery, and 74 mph at Aberporth. Stronger unofficial readings were reported from some exposed coastal locations. London Construction Magazine used the event to explain why a recorded gust cannot be treated as a direct temporary works design check.

Site teams are frequently asked whether a scaffold, hoarding, temporary roof or falsework is “rated for 70 mph” or similar. Without the design basis that question cannot be answered. Wind design accounts for site location, terrain, altitude, topography, neighbouring buildings, height, exposed area, porosity and the intended duration. An open scaffold, a scaffold with debris netting and a fully sheeted scaffold are not equivalent. Added banners, temporarily removed ties, altered hoarding panels, materials stored on platforms never designed for them, or the loss of shielding from demolition can all change the condition assumed by the original design. BS 5975-2:2024 specifically addresses effects of adjacent tall structures, funnelling and vortex shedding for falsework. The design is only valid for the arrangement that was checked.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify temporary works particularly exposed to wind (tall scaffolds, sheeted or netted elevations, temporary roofs, hoardings, façade retention, large formwork and falsework).
Confirm that the temporary works register, approved design, inspection status and the arrangement actually standing on site still describe the same structure.

Verify that ties, bracing, anchors and foundations remain as designed. Any temporary removal of ties or restraint is a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.

Establish whether sheeting, netting, banners or other surfaces have been added or altered since the design was checked. HSE scaffolding guidance is clear that sheeting or debris netting should not be attached without informing those responsible for the design.
Secure loose materials, boards and components that could become wind-borne. Follow any structure-specific or manufacturer operating restrictions.

Before severe wind, apply the project procedure for stopping or restricting work. NASC SG46:24 addresses weather-related risk assessment, stopping and resuming scaffold operations, inspection requirements and securing structures.

After high winds (or other circumstances liable to jeopardise safety), arrange inspection by a competent person appropriate to the type and complexity of the temporary works before normal use resumes. On scaffolding this includes ties, bracing, platforms, sheeting, base plates, sole boards and any evidence of movement or settlement. Heavy rain may also affect ground conditions under foundations even where no damage is obvious above ground.

Where a design assumption has changed, or where damage or partial dismantling leaves the installed arrangement different from the approved design, refer the issue back through the project temporary works procedure rather than resolving it informally on site.

NASC TG20:21 provides recognised scaffold configurations; TG30:24 addresses operational guidance. NASC SG46:24 addresses adverse and inclement weather. HSE scaffolding guidance requires ties to remain within safe working limits and scaffolds to be checked when substantially altered or adversely affected, including by high winds. On 18 December 2024, while a team was dismantling scaffold on a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, a metal scaffolding board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the structure and fell about 8 m. It struck Samuel Magill, 60, a collection driver employed by the company who had arrived to collect dismantled components. He had parked on the pavement and walked toward the work area. He was struck at the outer edge of the site exclusion zone, next to the pavement. He died in hospital on 5 February 2025.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone around the scaffolding during dismantling, so that people not directly involved in the work could approach. Inspector Kevin Campbell stated the incident was entirely preventable and that employers must ensure robust procedures so equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, with clear work instructions communicated to all relevant personnel, and a clear identified exclusion zone with measures to prevent unauthorised persons entering. Scaffold dismantling is a temporary works activity. Falling objects and people entering the drop zone are foreseeable risks under the Work at Height Regulations and CDM 2015. Collection and delivery activity must be planned into the method, not treated as separate.

ul: Every scaffold (including system and tube-and-fitting) is entered on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC, a design or TG20 compliance sheet, and an assembly, use and dismantling plan that specifically covers striking.
The dismantling plan requires controlled lowering of boards, tubes and fittings (gin wheel, hoist or equivalent). Throwing is not an acceptable method.

A physical exclusion zone is established below the work, clearly signed, and controlled by barriers or marshals so that drivers, other trades, visitors and the public cannot enter. The zone must account for the actual drop path, including items that can bounce or travel beyond the scaffold footprint.

Everyone who will be near the scaffold during dismantling — including collection drivers — is briefed on the zone and the method. A person whose role is to keep others out must not themselves be required to enter the zone.

Ties, bracing and platforms that maintain stability of the remaining scaffold are removed only in the planned sequence. Any departure is treated as a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
A competent person inspects the scaffold before dismantling starts and the permit-to-dismantle (or equivalent) is issued under the project temporary works procedure.

NASC SG4 addresses the scaffolders’ safe zone during erection and dismantling. HSE HSG150 (Health and safety in construction) addresses exclusion zones and preventing materials falling onto people. body.h: Why this is a temporary works prompt
body.p: Until the permanent structure is self-stable, construction sequence, temporary bracing, propping, scaffolding interfaces and any alteration to the load path are temporary works. HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads, and that structures should never be overloaded. Items that affect stability belong on the Temporary Works Register under the project procedure (BS 5975-1:2024).

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a late contractor change on a filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs, beams were to be lifted individually. Assessment showed utilisation exceeding 200% without rotational restraint and temporary LTB restraints. The Category II checker identified the issue; temporary restraints were required. The report notes that late changes to construction sequence can introduce significant temporary stability risks and that the Temporary Works Coordinator role must ensure clarity of design responsibility at each stage.

Revisions to the Building Safety section reflect that scaffolding and temporary works no longer fall within the scope of the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the clarification after seeking confirmation from MHCLG. Companies will opt out of the Building Safety section where it does not apply, with a confirming statement. ul: Every item that can affect structural stability during construction (scaffolding that is load-bearing or tied in a way that affects the permanent structure, temporary bracing, propping, sequence-critical elements) is on the Temporary Works Register with a named Temporary Works Coordinator.
There is a design or documented standard solution, an appropriate design check, a permit-to-load/use and a recent inspection by a person competent for that item.

Any proposed change to sequence, removal of bracing or props, or alteration of loading is treated as a design change and is not implemented until the temporary works designer confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.

body.p: On 14 October 2026 Construction Magazine / London Construction Magazine published “Before Scaffolding Is Erected: The Temporary Works Checks That Matter”. The article states that before a scaffold is erected the project team needs to know more than its height, length and intended access route. A scaffold can be correctly designed in isolation and still be unsuitable for the site if the ground, supporting structure, façade, services, attachments or future alterations do not match the assumptions used in that design. Problems commonly arise when elements are considered separately: leg loads bearing over a basement or void, increased reactions from a loading bay, mismatched tie patterns after façade removal, or wind actions from sheeting or temporary roofs that were not in the original brief. The current management procedures for temporary works are set out in BS 5975-1:2024. For project teams operating a BS 5975 procedure, the design brief is the point where requirements and interfaces should be captured before design progresses. Pre-erection checks cover design status (compliance sheet or project-specific design and check), intended loading, maximum leg reactions, foundation condition (including subsurface features), ties and anchors matched to the actual façade, attachments that affect loading or wind, site interfaces, and a change-control process.

Scaffolding is temporary works. HSE scaffolding guidance requires a scaffold either to follow a recognised standard configuration or, where it falls outside such a configuration, to be designed by calculation by a competent person. The foundation must be capable of carrying the scaffold and the loads placed on it; basements, drains and patches of soft ground that may collapse when loaded are specifically highlighted. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the industry framework for temporary works management procedures (it is not a statute). Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The design brief is the control point that brings together use, loads, reactions, ground or structural support, ties, attachments and foreseeable change so that the load path from the scaffold through bases and ties into the supporting ground or structure is coherent. Standard does not automatically mean low risk when site conditions differ from the assumptions behind a standard configuration. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Capture in the design brief the intended use, loading class, boarded lifts, material storage, loading bays, ties, sheeting/netting, hoists, debris chutes, temporary roofs, ground conditions, subsurface features, façade type and any planned alterations before design or erection proceeds.
Confirm design status: either a recognised standard configuration whose assumptions are valid for the site, or a project-specific design and independent check by a competent person.

Obtain maximum leg reactions (including concentrated loads) and assess the supporting ground or structure. Treat basements, drains, manholes, voids, soft patches or recently backfilled ground as requiring specific assessment rather than assuming surface adequacy.
Verify that the tie strategy matches the actual façade, including openings, curtain walling, weak masonry or planned removals. Confirm anchor type, substrate suitability and any testing requirements.
Identify attachments (sheeting, netting, hoists, loading bays, fans, temporary roofs) as design inputs so that their effect on reactions, wind loading and restraint is allowed for before erection.

Establish change control so that any alteration to geometry, loading, restraint, exposure, foundations or supporting structure is referred to the Temporary Works Coordinator and re-checked where necessary before it is adopted.
Where the scaffold interfaces with public highways, excavations, deliveries or other temporary works, confirm licences, clearances and sequencing are compatible with the checked arrangement.

At permit-to-load or equivalent, confirm that the erected arrangement matches the design brief and checked design, including foundations, ties and attachments. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1479, published on 13 January 2026, concerns a filler beam bridge deck of approximately 20 m span. During the final stages of design and shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor changed the intended construction sequence. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with the concrete infill precast to provide temporary stability for each pair), the beams were to be lifted individually. The change introduced a significant temporary stability concern: the risk of lateral-torsional buckling of the beams under the weight of the wet concrete applied during construction. The Category II checker identified that the main beams, if left unbraced and without rotational restraint at the ends of the flanges, could experience buckling under a utilisation factor of over 200%. Discussions involved commercial and programme considerations around design responsibility. Eventually the permanent works designer prepared a bracing scheme that tied the inner girders back to the precast edge beams, but by that stage most of the deck reinforcement had been fixed, restricting available space. HSE temporary works guidance further requires that any temporary structure is designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads and is only used for the purposes for which it was designed. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures for the control of temporary works as recognised industry good practice (it is not a statute). Late changes to erection or construction sequences can alter the temporary stability condition in ways that are not covered by the permanent works design assumptions. Independent checking and clear communication between permanent works designers, temporary works designers and the Temporary Works Coordinator are essential to identify such risks before they reach site. body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by chartered civil engineer Vicky Mastoridou (CEng, MICE), development manager at Groundforce Shorco, titled “Redefining geotechnical limits: thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works”. The article examines the geotechnical impact of extreme heat cycles on soil mechanics and the structural implications of thermal expansion in propping systems. It observes that with the summer of 2026 again surpassing previous temperature benchmarks, sustained thermal loads over 30 °C, widespread desiccation and shifting water tables can no longer be treated as short-term weather anomalies. Historical return periods based on past climate baselines cease to offer a reliable basis when extreme events recur. In clay-rich formations such as London Clay, extended dry spells cause the ground to shrink and crack, temporarily increasing stiffness while allowing movements that can affect foundations and excavations. When intense rainfall follows, water enters the cracks rapidly, producing localised softening, swelling and changes in pore-water conditions. Lateral earth pressures behind retaining structures can therefore spike more quickly than conventional design models anticipate. For temporary works this means ground parameters assumed at design stage may not remain valid during construction. Separately, exposed structural steelwork (heavy-duty hydraulic props, sheet piling and bracing frames) absorbs solar radiation, driving surface temperatures above ambient. Because these elements are restrained between retaining walls, walers and concrete slabs they cannot expand freely. The restraint converts thermal energy into compressive axial forces. A hydraulic prop operating under static earth pressures can experience a sharp load spike purely due to thermal expansion, transferring additional loading into the retaining structure and consuming part of the resistance reserve calculated under BS EN 1997 (Eurocode 7) partial factors. To accommodate the thermal component without exceeding design resistance, stronger, larger or denser propping layouts may be required, reducing working clearance. Distinguishing actual ground movement from thermal load spikes requires careful interpretation of telemetry from load cells.

Temporary works are an engineered solution used to support or protect a structure during construction, retain the sides of an excavation, or provide access. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. HSE temporary works guidance states that the law requires any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads which may be imposed on it and that it be only used for the purposes for which it was designed, installed and maintained. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures for the control of temporary works as industry good practice; it is not a statute. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Eurocode 7 (BS EN 1997) is the basis for geotechnical design of retaining structures and their temporary support, including consideration of actions arising from temperature changes in struts or props. body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State in the design brief the expected period of use, the range of ambient and surface temperatures that may be encountered, the ground conditions (including susceptibility to desiccation or rapid wetting), and whether thermal expansion of restrained props or frames has been considered.

Include heat, desiccation or rapid wetting as review triggers under the project temporary works procedure. After a period of elevated temperature or intense rainfall, inspect and, where necessary, stop and review before continued reliance on the support system.

Confirm that any denser or stronger propping required to accommodate thermal effects still provides the required working space, access and plant logistics, or that the method has been adjusted accordingly.

At permit-to-load and during routine inspection, verify that the installed arrangement matches the design assumptions, including any measures (coating, shading, hydraulic compensation or monitoring) specified to manage thermal effects.
Do not proceed until the arrangement, including thermal and moisture assumptions, has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: HSE’s Temporary works FAQs state that the same degree of care and attention must be given to the design and construction of temporary works as to the permanent works. Because temporary works may be in place for only a short while, there is a tendency to assume they are less important. This is incorrect. Lack of care with design, selection, assembly and so on leaves temporary works liable to fail or collapse, placing people at risk of injury and causing project delay. The same guidance notes that temporary works can be very sensitive to how they are used and are easily affected by other work taking place nearby, and that failure is often found to result from the loadings being underestimated. HSE describes coordinating temporary works as including planning where and when they will be needed and ensuring they are correctly installed, used, checked and maintained. On 9 October 2026 EE&HL Network published an insight titled “When Temporary Works Stay in Place Too Long”. It observes that temporary works design and management depend on the loads, the conditions and the anticipated period of use. When the programme moves, the load is still checked; the period of use is not always revisited. A longer temporary state can meet more weather, more nearby activity, more changes of crew and more opportunities for an adjacent trade to lean on it, remove a brace or load it in a way nobody considered. The insight lists typical causes (weather windows slipping, plant or crew not ready, another scope finishing first, open decisions deferred to site) and notes that the UK framework already provides for coordination across the whole life of the temporary works. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out management procedures and the Temporary Works Coordinator role as industry good practice; HSE notes there is no legal requirement to use that job title, but that the Standard provides a consensus view of good practice.

Temporary works are an engineered solution used to support or protect a structure during construction, support plant or equipment, retain the sides of an excavation, or provide access. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out a temporary works procedure as industry good practice; it is not a statute. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The period of use is an assumption that belongs in the design brief. When that period is exceeded because the programme has moved, the temporary works may be meeting conditions that were not the basis of the original design, check or inspection regime. Standard does not automatically mean low risk when the temporary state has outlived its brief. A prop, brace, falsework tower or excavation support that was adequate for a planned few weeks can become higher consequence if it remains in place through additional weather events, adjacent trade activity or unconsidered loading. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State the expected period of use, the design loads, the weather and adjacent-activity assumptions, and the inspection and maintenance regime in the design brief before the temporary works are designed.
Treat any extension of the planned period of use as a change that requires review under the project temporary works procedure before the temporary works continue to be relied upon.
Send the extended period, the revised adjacent activities and any changed loading or weather exposure back to the temporary works designer and checker.
Confirm that the original assumptions still hold, or that a revised design/check has been accepted, before loading or continued use is permitted.
Include the whole life of the temporary works (installation, use, checking, maintenance and removal) in the coordination role. Do not treat design acceptance as the end of control.
After adverse weather, nearby activity, crew changes or any event that could affect stability, inspect and, where necessary, stop and review before work continues.
At the point of removal or striking, confirm that the permanent structure is ready to take the load and that the removal sequence itself has been reviewed.
Do not proceed until the arrangement, including any extended period, has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1525, published 13 May 2026, records a reporter’s concern about the continued use on sites of ad hoc timber bracing systems that support masonry walls under construction. These arrangements lack a proper temporary works design, calculations or oversight, leaving structures unstable and workers exposed to serious risk. The reporter notes that principal contractors are often not effectively communicating with Temporary Works Coordinators and are failing to identify or request temporary works designs within bricklayers’ work packages. Temporary works are installed informally without design, approval or control. The Expert Panel confirms that temporary stability of masonry walls during construction is a well-recognised safety concern because partially completed walls can be vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads such as wind, impact or construction activities. Collapses of masonry walls during construction have historically resulted in serious injuries and fatalities. Ad hoc or improvised bracing may represent an attempt to address a recognised risk but does not provide a reliable or consistent level of restraint, and poorly conceived temporary works can introduce additional hazards. The Panel stresses that temporary works should be properly identified and managed in accordance with established procedures such as those set out in BS 5975. HSE temporary works guidance states that the law requires any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads which may be imposed on it and that it be only used for the purposes for which it was designed, installed and maintained. The same control failure was present in the Paxton House incident (23 February 2024; fines confirmed June 2026): temporary wooden platforms used to collect concrete cores and debris during floor openings had no design and no calculation of safe loading. An inspection form was completed by a person who was not a competent temporary works coordinator. Roots Contractors Limited and Diacutt Limited were fined after a drilling operative sustained fractures to his neck and back.

Temporary works are an engineered solution used to support or protect a structure during construction, support plant or equipment, retain the sides of an excavation, or provide access. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out a temporary works procedure as industry good practice; it is not a statute. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. When temporary restraint of a masonry wall, or any temporary support or platform, is required, that item belongs on the temporary works register. If the residual structure, the bracing arrangement, the loads (wind, impact, construction activity, adjacent trade interference) or the period of use needs assessment, it needs a design brief and competent design/check under the project procedure. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. An improvised timber brace that has “always been used” is not low risk if its capacity under the actual loads has not been assessed. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify temporary restraint or bracing of masonry walls under construction as a temporary works item on the register before the wall rises beyond the height that can stand unsupported.

The design brief should state the wall height and thickness, the expected loads (wind, impact, construction activity), the period the temporary state will exist, the interface with scaffolding or adjacent trades, and the hold points for inspection and removal.
Avoid improvised or ad-hoc timber bracing that has not been assessed. Use proven proprietary systems or a designed arrangement that has been checked under the project procedure.
Confirm competence of the people erecting, inspecting and altering the bracing, and that the arrangement has been accepted under the project temporary works procedure before it is relied upon.
Do not allow progressive construction of the wall while the temporary support remains informal or unreviewed.
After any change (brace moved, adjacent activity introduced, weather event, wall height increased), treat it as a change that requires review before work continues.
At the point of removal, confirm that the permanent structure (floors, roofs, cross-walls or other permanent restraint) is in place and ready to provide the required stability.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 2 October 2026 the Health and Safety Executive Media Centre published the outcome of the prosecution of W G Carter Limited of Appleton, Oxfordshire. Richard “Felix” Roper, a 59-year-old father of two, died after falling from the first floor of Manor Barn House, Nether Westcote, Gloucestershire, on 30 August 2022. He had been tasked with replacing damaged floor joists while other workers removed sections of flooring in the same area. Extensive repairs were under way to replace rotten floor joists and floorboards. Large parts of the first-floor structure had been stripped back, leaving open gaps between joists. Some joists were either missing altogether or had not been secured. Mr Roper fell to the concrete ground floor below, sustained severe head injuries and died in hospital the following day. A joint investigation by HSE and Gloucestershire Police found that the work at height had not been properly planned, appropriately supervised or carried out safely. Workers, including Mr Roper, were able to access areas where flooring and structural supports had been removed despite insufficient measures to prevent falls. Other workers were continuing to remove floorboards, creating and increasing the risk. Following the incident HSE served a Prohibition Notice stopping further work at height until adequate safety measures had been introduced. The company later adopted a safer method: installing floor joists from below using appropriate work-at-height equipment and preventing access to the first floor while the work was undertaken. On 24 September 2026 at Bristol Magistrates Court the company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. It was fined £120,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,247. HSE principal inspector James Lucas said that due to the failings of the company a man lost his life, and that every year workers are killed or suffer life-changing injuries because work at height has not been properly planned or suitable safeguards have not been put in place.

Falls from height remain a leading cause of death in construction. Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005 requires every employer to ensure that work at height is properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out in a manner that is, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. In a refurbishment where the existing floor is being removed or opened, the temporary condition of that floor — open gaps, missing or unsecured joists, sequence of removal, residual load-carrying capacity of what remains, and the protection or access arrangement that replaces it — is a temporary works item. It belongs on the temporary works register. If the residual structure or the temporary protection (crash deck, boarding, edge protection, alternative access from below) needs assessment, it needs a design brief and competent design/check under the project procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out a temporary works procedure as industry good practice; it is not a statute. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. An arrangement that looks simple (boards being removed, joists replaced) can become high consequence when people are working on the structure that is being dismantled and there is no engineered temporary state. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify floor-opening, joist-removal or partial-demolition of floors as a temporary works item on the register before work starts. Do not treat it as ordinary carpentry.

The design brief should state the sequence, the residual structure that remains, the temporary protection or alternative access method, the loads (people, tools, materials), the public or occupied interface if any, and the hold points.

Prefer prevention of the fall: sequence the work so that access to the open floor is prevented, install joists or supports from below where practicable, or provide a designed temporary platform / crash deck / boarded working surface that is controlled under the procedure.
Do not allow progressive removal of boards and joists while people continue to work on the same floor without a reviewed temporary arrangement.

Edge protection, boarding or exclusion must be in place before the surface is opened. Inspection and maintenance of that temporary state belongs in the ITP or permit-to-load / permit-to-work arrangements.
After any alteration (further boards removed, joists cut, temporary boarding moved), treat it as a change that requires review before work continues.
Confirm competence of the people carrying out and supervising the work, and that the temporary arrangement has been accepted under the project temporary works procedure before access is permitted.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry view by Vicky Mastoridou (CEng, MICE), development manager at Groundforce Shorco, titled Redefining geotechnical limits: thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works. The piece notes that the summer of 2026 again surpassed previous temperature benchmarks, with sustained thermal loads over 30°C, widespread desiccation and shifting water tables no longer treatable as short-term weather anomalies. In clay-rich formations such as London Clay, extended dry spells can shrink and crack the ground, altering stiffness and strength. Subsequent intense rainfall can penetrate those cracks rapidly, causing localised softening, swelling and pore-water pressure changes. Lateral earth pressures behind retaining structures can therefore rise faster than conventional design models anticipate. For temporary works this means ground parameters assumed at design may not remain valid through construction. At the same time, exposed structural steelwork (hydraulic props, sheet piling, bracing frames) absorbs solar radiation, raising surface temperatures above ambient. Because these members are restrained between retaining walls, walers and slabs they cannot expand freely; thermal energy converts into additional compressive axial forces. A strut specified to resist active earth pressure must simultaneously resist geotechnical thrust and its own restrained thermal expansion, consuming part of the structural resistance calculated under partial factors. The practical consequence can be a requirement for stronger, larger or denser propping layouts, reducing working clearance. Distinguishing actual ground movement from thermal load spikes requires careful interpretation of load-cell data.

Temporary works are not a short-lived exception to the duty to plan, manage and monitor construction work. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure; it is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. When the climatic envelope assumed in the design brief is exceeded, the ground parameters, earth pressures and thermal loads that justified the scheme, the inspection frequency and the monitoring regime may no longer hold. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary propping or shoring system whose published capacity was calculated for a defined set of ground and temperature conditions is not low risk if the actual conditions have already moved outside that envelope and the brief has not been revisited. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State the expected climatic envelope (temperature range, duration of exposure, rainfall after dry periods) and the trigger for formal review if that envelope is exceeded in the design brief and on the temporary works register entry.
When heatwave conditions, desiccation or rapid rainfall occur, treat the change as a potential alteration to the temporary works assumptions. Send it back for review before the works simply continue.
Where load cells or other instrumentation are installed, record both load and temperature so thermal spikes can be distinguished from ground movement. Do not rely on a visual check alone.
Confirm that the person inspecting has the competence and authority required by the project procedure to interpret changes in load or ground conditions.
If denser or higher-capacity propping is required to accommodate thermal load, confirm that working space, access and plant movements remain acceptable under the revised arrangement.
At the point of removal or alteration, confirm that the permanent structure (or the next temporary state) is ready to take the load under the current ground and temperature conditions.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 EE&HL Network published an insight by Marco Torri titled When Temporary Works Stay in Place Too Long. The piece observes that temporary works design and management depend on the loads, the conditions and the anticipated period of use. The load is written down and checked. The period of use is often an assumption in the background: the supports will be there for a few weeks, the propping until the slab gains strength, the tower until the stays are in. When the programme moves, the load is still checked. The period of use is not always revisited. HSE’s guidance on temporary works names the attitude behind this: because temporary works may be in place for only a short while, there is a tendency to assume they are less important. The same guidance notes that temporary works can be sensitive to how they are used and to work going on nearby, and that failures are often linked to loadings that were underestimated. A temporary state that lasts longer than planned can meet more weather, more nearby activity, more changes of crew and more opportunities for an adjacent trade to lean on it, remove a brace or load it in a way nobody considered. Typical causes include weather windows slipping, plant or crew not being ready, another scope having to finish first, and open design or method decisions being deferred to site. Documented projects such as the Millau Viaduct (release of temporary towers dependent on stay-cable installation) and the Krk Bridge (arch halves standing on tie-backs until the crown closed) illustrate how the life of temporary works is set by something other than the temporary works themselves. HSE describes temporary works coordination as including making sure temporary works are correctly installed, used, checked and maintained across their whole life. BS 5975 sets out the temporary works co-ordinator role as industry good practice; HSE notes that there is no legal requirement to use that job title. A practical reading is that a change in programme can affect the assumptions in the temporary works brief and is worth sending back to whoever designed and checked them.

Temporary works are not a short-lived exception to the duty to plan, manage and monitor construction work. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure; it is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The design brief should state the expected period of use. When that period is exceeded, or when the programme changes in a way that affects weather exposure, adjacent activities, loading or the sequence of removal, the assumptions that justified the design, the inspection frequency and the maintenance regime may no longer hold. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary falsework or propping system whose published capacity was calculated for a defined short duration is not low risk if the actual occupation has already exceeded that duration and the brief has not been revisited. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State the expected period of use, and the trigger for formal review if that period is exceeded, in the design brief and on the temporary works register entry.

When the programme slips, or when weather, access or an interface with another contractor extends the temporary state, treat that extension as a potential change to the temporary works. Send it back for review before the works simply continue.
Do not assume that a daily visual check remains sufficient if the duration, exposure or adjacent activity has changed. Record the inspection and note any change in conditions.
Confirm that the person inspecting has the competence and authority required by the project procedure. A glance that does not consider duration is incomplete.
If adjacent trades, plant or storage begin to interact with the temporary works in a way not considered in the original brief, stop and re-assess before the interaction becomes the norm.
At the point of removal or alteration, confirm that the permanent structure (or the next temporary state) is ready to take the load. Removal is not automatically lower risk than installation.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 October 2026 Ground Engineering published an industry-view article by Vicky Mastoridou CEng MICE, development manager at Groundforce Shorco, titled Redefining geotechnical limits: thermal loading and soil volatility in temporary works. The piece argues that record-breaking heatwaves and the summer of 2026 have exposed a design vulnerability: temporary works and shoring schemes are increasingly required to operate beyond the climatic envelopes assumed at design. Sustained temperatures above 30°C, widespread desiccation and shifting water tables can no longer be treated as short-term weather anomalies. In clay-rich formations such as London Clay, extended dry spells cause shrinkage and cracking that change stiffness and strength. Subsequent intense rainfall then penetrates those cracks rapidly, producing localised softening, swelling and pore-water conditions that can spike lateral earth pressures faster than conventional models anticipate. At the same time, exposed structural steelwork — hydraulic props, sheet piles and bracing frames — absorbs direct solar radiation, driving surface temperatures above ambient. Because these members are restrained between retaining walls, walers and slabs they cannot expand freely; the restraint converts thermal energy into additional compressive axial force. That force consumes part of the structural resistance calculated under BS EN 1997 partial factors. To remain within capacity, designers may need to specify stronger or denser propping layouts, which reduces internal working clearance. The article concludes that the critical question is no longer whether a heatwave is likely, but how the temporary works will perform under the extreme event, and that ground assessment, thermal modelling and real-time monitoring should be embedded from the start.

Excavation support, propping and temporary retaining structures are temporary works. Their performance depends on both the ground parameters assumed in the design brief and the loads the support system itself must carry. CDM 2015 requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure; it is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. BS EN 1997-1 and its UK National Annex govern geotechnical design; the partial factors and load combinations used for temporary states should be those appropriate to the temporary works design, not simply copied from a permanent-works calculation. A ground investigation carried out in winter or spring does not automatically remain valid through a prolonged heatwave and subsequent rainfall. Desiccation cracking followed by rapid infiltration can change undrained strength, stiffness and pore pressures within the life of the temporary works. Thermal expansion in restrained props is an additional load case, not a secondary effect that can be ignored because the prop has a manufacturer’s capacity. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A proprietary hydraulic prop whose capacity is stated at a reference temperature is not low risk if the site has already recorded surface temperatures that generate axial forces consuming a substantial fraction of that capacity. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: State the expected temperature range, solar-gain exposure and the possibility of changing ground parameters (desiccation, subsequent rainfall, groundwater fluctuation) in the design brief for any propping or excavation-support scheme.
Require the temporary works designer to identify the thermal load component separately from the geotechnical load and to show the residual capacity available for earth pressure.
Do not treat a winter or spring ground investigation as sufficient for a summer construction phase without a review of whether desiccation or rainfall has altered the parameters used in the design.
Where load cells or monitoring are installed, ensure the interpretation method can distinguish a thermal spike from genuine ground movement. An alert that cannot be attributed is not a control.
If denser or stronger propping is required to accommodate thermal loads, confirm that the reduced working clearance is still compatible with the plant, access and sequence in the method statement.

Inspect and re-assess after any prolonged heat or heavy rainfall that could affect either the ground or the restrained steelwork. Record the inspection. A daily visual check that does not consider temperature is incomplete.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 9 September 2026, following a trial at the Old Bailey, principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited and subcontractor T Vaughan Limited were convicted of breaching Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Gheorghita Arsene, 33, died on 24 June 2020 at a site on Park Road, Banstead, Surrey when the walls of a deep trench collapsed while he was working at the bottom to replace a damaged pipe. The trench had been dug with a three-tonne digger. He was clearing soil with a shovel and a pickaxe when the sides failed. He was buried under approximately two tonnes of soil and died at the scene. A joint investigation by Surrey Police and the Health and Safety Executive found there were no supports in the trench and that excavated soil had been deposited immediately next to the edge. Earlier the same day Anthony O’Connor, a self-employed contracts manager working for T Vaughan Limited, had observed another worker in the same unsupported excavation. As an experienced contracts manager he knew suitable measures were required to prevent a collapse but failed to ensure they were implemented. T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 and ordered to pay costs of £40,000. Appledorn Developments Limited was fined £500,000. O’Connor pleaded guilty on 22 May 2026 to breaching Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, with 150 hours of unpaid work. The prosecution was brought by the Crown Prosecution Service. HSE does not set the fine.

An excavation that a person will enter, or that can affect persons or adjacent assets if it fails, is temporary works. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase, and requires contractors to plan, manage and monitor their own work. Regulation 22 of CDM 2015 specifically addresses excavations and requires suitable and sufficient steps to prevent them from collapsing or causing a person to be buried or trapped. Spoil deposited next to the crest is a surcharge load. The absence of support is not a neutral condition; it is an unsupported temporary face. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. The temporary works procedure should identify the excavation, require a design brief where the geometry, ground, surcharge or sequence makes a standard solution inadequate, and control the permit-to-enter and the inspection regime. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A short trench for a pipe replacement becomes high consequence the moment a person is working at the bottom with an unsupported face and a spoil heap at the edge. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Enter every excavation that a person will enter, or that can affect adjacent structures, services or the public, on the temporary works register. A digger ticket is not a register entry.

Confirm the design brief states depth, length, ground conditions, groundwater, existing services, adjacent structures and the surcharge from plant and spoil. Spoil must not be deposited next to the crest unless the design specifically allows it.

Do not allow entry until a suitable support system (trench box, sheets and frames, or other designed arrangement) is in place and the permit-to-enter has been issued. An unsupported face is not a temporary works solution.
The contracts manager who sees an unsupported excavation and walks past it is not the control. The control is the procedure that stops the work until the support is installed.

Inspect the support before each shift and after any event that could affect stability (heavy rain, plant movement, ground heave). Record the inspection. A daily visual glance without competence or authority is not an inspection.
If the sequence requires the support to be removed or altered to complete the pipe work, that change is a temporary works alteration. It requires review before it is made.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 29 September 2026 the Civil Engineering Contractors Association called on organisations across the built environment to take part in Stop. Make a Change 2026. The campaign runs throughout October. CECA asks employers, workers, clients and other organisations to pause work so people can take part in sessions on three areas: serious injuries and fatalities, serious work-related health conditions, and mental health. CECA states that the campaign has run every year since 2017, involving hundreds of its members, the wider sector and clients, and reaching tens of thousands of operatives. This year’s programme includes workplace substance misuse, trauma, safe driving, drug driving, mental health, the people–plant interface, and the use of AI and video technology. CECA describes itself as representing more than 300 members across England, Scotland and Wales, delivering around £20 billion of maintenance and improvements to transport and utility networks each year. Andrew Rippington, chair of the CECA Health, Safety and Wellbeing Group, said the campaign is about making a commitment, not only taking a pause, and pointed organisations to free events and resources. The campaign page does not publish a fatality table. The figures below are HSE’s, not CECA’s.

HSE published provisional work-related fatality statistics for 2025/26 on 1 July 2026. The release records 126 workers killed in work-related incidents. Construction accounts for 25 deaths, the largest number of any main industry sector, and agriculture, forestry and fishing for 22. Falls from a height account for 31 worker deaths, around a quarter of the total. Struck by a moving vehicle accounts for 24, struck by a moving object for 21, and trapped by something collapsing or overturning for 18. HSE states that the 2025/26 figures are provisional and will be finalised in July 2027. Excluding the pandemic years, HSE describes 2025/26 as provisionally the lowest annual total recorded. A lower national total is not a site control. For a contractor the relevant point is the kind of accident, not the ranking. A fall from an incomplete floor, a scaffold edge or a tower is temporary works and work at height. A person struck at a platform edge or in a plant exclusion is a working-platform and traffic-management interface. A collapse or overturn is the failure mode behind an unsupported excavation, a poorly founded outrigger and an unrestrained temporary structure. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require the work to be planned, supervised and carried out so far as is reasonably practicable safely. CDM 2015 requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. A campaign session is industry good practice. It is not a design, a check or a permit. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Use the October pause to walk the register, not only to deliver a talk. Each open edge, scaffold, platform, excavation and outrigger set-up should still have a brief, a check category and a permit status.
Do not treat a people–plant session as acceptance of the platform. A change of crane, pump, MEWP or delivery vehicle is a change of load and of exclusion.

Falls from a height remain the largest fatal accident kind in the provisional year. Incomplete floors, openings, strike sequence and scaffold edges stay on the register until the permanent protection is there.
Struck by a moving vehicle is the second largest kind. Platform edges, reversing zones and public interfaces need a drawing and a hold point, not a cone placed on the day.
Trapped by something collapsing or overturning is the excavation and temporary-stability line. Spoil at the crest, water, a missing box and an altered sequence are design changes until reviewed.
A domestic or small civils job is not exempt. The same accident kinds appear on refurbishment floors and short trenches.
AI or video used to watch an exclusion is a monitoring aid. It does not replace the competent person, the inspection or the permit to load.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.
