body.p: On 6 October 2026 the Health and Safety Executive reported that Daniel Watton, 50, trading as Inside Out Painters and Decorators Property Maintenance, was sentenced at Warrington Magistrates’ Court after trainee painter Connor Lambert was electrocuted. Lambert, 24, from Market Drayton, died on 29 July 2024 while working at a house in Farndon. HSE’s investigation found that he and a colleague were moving a fully extended ladder at the gable end. During that move the ladder either came into contact with an overhead power line or came close enough for an electrical arc to form. Lambert was killed. His colleague suffered burns to his hands, feet and stomach. HSE found that the work at height had not been properly planned, supervised or carried out safely, that the equipment and methods were unsuitable, and that the risks from the overhead line had not been adequately assessed or controlled. The investigation also identified issues with the training and competence of those doing the work. The original plan used a tower scaffold and ladders to paint the exterior, including an area with a glass canopy. HSE found that approach neither suitable nor safe. In practice the work departed from the plan and ladders were used throughout. That method was approved by Watton and was also unsuitable and unsafe. He pleaded guilty to breaching regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The court imposed 16 weeks’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and ordered him to pay £10,645 in costs. HSE inspector Keeley Eves said work at height and work near overhead power lines are both high-risk activities, and that suitable equipment, a full assessment and trained, supervised workers are required. HSE does not set the sentence.

This was a domestic painting job. The failure mode is the same one that appears on a civils site when a long object is walked under a line: the access method and the electrical interface were never one control. A tower scaffold written into a plan is temporary works equipment. It still has to be suitable for the place it stands, including a glass canopy, and it still has to be erected, altered and used by people who are competent for that configuration. A ladder used instead is a change of method. Approving that change without reassessing the line is how the original plan stops being the control. Work at Height Regulations 2005, regulation 4(1), requires the work to be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out in a manner which is so far as is reasonably practicable safe. Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require electrical systems and work on or near them to be controlled so as to prevent danger. HSE’s GS6 is industry guidance on avoiding danger from overhead power lines, not a statute. CDM 2015 still requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored where it applies, including on a domestic client project through the contractor duties. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for a temporary works procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. A mobile tower is not low risk because it is a standard product. Wind, ground, overhead lines, a canopy and a move of a long conductor all change the consequence. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Treat a tower scaffold, a podium and a ladder used for access as items on the temporary works or access register. A domestic client does not take them off the register.
Before the method is accepted, mark the overhead lines, the exclusion zone and the longest object that will be moved. A fully extended ladder is a long conductor.
Do not approve a departure from a tower to ladders without a new assessment. The original plan is not a permit for the method used on the day.

Where work near a line cannot be avoided, the hierarchy is isolation or diversion by the network operator, then distance and suitable equipment. A goalpost or barrier is a control only if it is in the brief and used.
A tower that cannot be stood clear of the line, or that cannot be erected without the ladder entering the zone, is the wrong equipment for that elevation. Do not force the sheet to fit.
Competence is part of the brief. Training and supervision for the people moving the access equipment belong in the permit, not in a card on the file.
A glass canopy, soft ground or a public footpath is an interface. The tower base and the exclusion both have to be accepted before load.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: NASC’s Safety Report 2026 is based on RIDDOR returns from contractor members for the 2025 calendar year. The President’s welcome records that there were no operative fatalities among NASC contractor members in 2025. The fatalities section repeats that: there were no fatalities to operatives working for NASC contractor members in 2025. Members reported 82 RIDDORs from a combined workforce of 20,168 operatives, employed by 332 contractor members. The accident incident rate was 4.07 per 1,000 operatives and the accident frequency rate was 0.21 per 100,000 hours, which the report states corresponds to about one RIDDOR per 470,000 work hours. Of the 82, 28 were specified injuries and 54 were over-seven-day. Slips and trips on the same level were the most common cause, with 25 accidents. Manual handling was second, with 20. Falls from height of persons were third, with 17. Of the specified injuries, falls from height by persons accounted for eight (29 per cent) and slips and trips on the same level for eight (29 per cent). The report also records one incident involving a member of the public that a member reported to HSE as a RIDDOR. NASC’s review of the information supplied did not consider that it met the RIDDOR criteria, but it is included because it was reported to both HSE and NASC. No incidents involving injuries to third parties were reported. NASC states that HSE construction industry fatality statistics were the highest of all sectors in 2025, with 35 fatal injuries, and notes that NASC reporting runs January to December while HSE reporting runs April to March. Scottish Construction News reported the publication on 6 October 2026, including NASC’s statement that the report coincides with NASC Safety Day. This briefing uses the report’s own figures. It does not treat a membership audit as a project check.

A year with no operative fatality inside a membership scheme is a performance record. It is not evidence that the next scaffold is suitable. Seventeen falls of persons, and eight specified injuries from those falls, sit in the same return as the zero. Slips and trips on the same level were the largest group, which is a platform, access and housekeeping problem as much as a harness problem. On a UK site a scaffold is temporary works: configured to the manufacturer’s instructions or a TG20 compliance sheet, or designed where it is outside that sheet, then checked and permitted under the project temporary works procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for that procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require the work to be planned, supervised and carried out by competent people, with measures that prevent a fall where that is reasonably practicable. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s scaffolding guidance expects erection, alteration and dismantling by competent people, and inspection before first use, after alteration, after an event that may have affected stability, and at intervals not exceeding seven days. NASC membership, an audit and a safety report do not replace that inspection or the permit to load. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Public interface, incomplete structure, sheeting, loading and ties into a building that is still being altered can take a common scaffold out of a default low category. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put every scaffold on the temporary works register, including a tied independent, a tower and a loading bay. A trade-body member supplying it does not take it off the register.
Match the elevation to the TG20 sheet or the system design. If height, ties, sheeting, loading or the supporting structure are outside the sheet, it is a designed item.
Do not treat zero fatalities in a membership year as a reason to skip the design brief, the check or the permit to load.
Falls of persons were still 17 of the 82 RIDDORs. Control open edges, incomplete lifts and strike sequence before the harness is treated as the control.
Slips and trips were the largest group. Boarding, traps, access and material on the platform belong in the inspection, not only in a toolbox talk.
A tie into a building that is being stripped, altered or not yet at strength is an interface. Accept the tie only against the structure that is actually there.
Where the public can be under or beside the scaffold, exclusion and stability are both required. One public report in the return is a reminder, not a clean sheet.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

Membership figures and rates are as stated by NASC. They are not a site-specific risk assessment, a design check or a statement that a non-member scaffold is unsuitable. posts.title: An access scaffold is not the formwork — the HS2 dive-under is a designed interface
posts.excerpt: Scaffmag reported on 29 September 2026 that PERI UK is supplying access scaffold, wall formwork and high-level bracket platforms for Balfour Beatty VINCI’s Birmingham Spur Dive-Under, where reinforced concrete walls rise to 11 m. PERI UP Flex platforms are being used for reinforcement to those walls. VARIO girder formwork is configured with closer spacing for the taller pours, and pressure sensors on selected pours are being compared with the design pressures. SCS brackets anchored to the completed walls then provide the roof-slab edge platform. For contractors the lesson is the interface: access, formwork and bracket platforms are separate temporary works items, even when one supplier coordinates the drawings.

body.p: On 29 September 2026 Scaffmag reported that PERI UK is supplying temporary works equipment for the Birmingham Spur Dive-Under, delivered by Balfour Beatty VINCI as part of HS2 Delta Junction, north-east of Birmingham. The structure lets one high-speed line pass beneath another. Its main reinforced concrete walls rise to 11 m. PERI UP Flex modular scaffolding is providing access and support around the high wall sections, and access platforms from that system are being used by teams installing reinforcement to the 11 m walls. Scaffmag records that PERI says its scaffold and formwork designs were coordinated by its engineering teams before arriving on site, to reduce clashes between the temporary works systems. For the wall pours, Balfour Beatty VINCI is using PERI VARIO girder wall formwork, which can be configured with closer spacing between girders, walers and ties for the loads from the taller pours. Concrete pressure sensors have been installed on selected wall pours so the team can monitor loads on the formwork and compare them with the pressures calculated at design stage. The wider package described includes MAXIMO panel formwork for foundation works and BECOSTOP stop ends where reinforcement congestion made conventional timber stop ends difficult. As work moves to the roof slab, PERI SCS brackets can be anchored directly to the completed 11 m walls to create high-level working platforms for reinforcement and to support the formwork at the roof-slab edge. Scaffmag records that this removes the need for the working platform to be supported from ground level and avoids ties passing through the finished concrete. Dan Biggs, senior sales engineer at PERI UK, is quoted on the practical benefit of taking accessories, scaffolding and formwork from one supplier. This briefing does not endorse that equipment. It uses the published arrangement as an interface example.

Access, formwork and a bracket platform fixed to young concrete are three temporary works items that share a face. Treating them as one “scaffold package” is how load gets into the wrong member. An access scaffold to BS EN 12811-1 is there to carry people, materials for the stated duty and the environmental actions in its design. It is not, by that fact, falsework or formwork to BS EN 12812 or the formwork sections of BS 5975. Pour pressure, tie loads and the reaction from a slab-edge form belong in the formwork design. A bracket anchored into the wall transfers that platform load into concrete whose age, strength and anchor capacity have to be in the brief. HSE’s temporary works guidance expects any temporary structure to be designed, installed and maintained for the foreseeable loads, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for the management procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. A supplier coordinating its own drawings reduces clash risk. It does not appoint the project Temporary Works Coordinator, and it does not replace the design check or the permit to load. Standard does not automatically mean low risk: an 11 m wall pour, public or railway interface, and a change of support from ground scaffold to wall bracket are all reasons to confirm the category. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register the access scaffold, the wall formwork and the bracket platform as separate items, with a named interface: who owns the shared face, the ties and the anchors.
Do not let the access scaffold carry formwork, pour pressure or slab-edge reactions unless that load is in its design and check. Duty class on a TG20 or system sheet is not a pour-load design.
Brief wall height, pour rate, concrete temperature, tie layout and the design pressure. Closer girder and tie spacing is a design output, not a site preference on the day.
If pressure sensors are used, state what they are for: comparison with the design pressure, and the action if the reading approaches the limit. A sensor is not a permit.
For brackets anchored to completed walls, hold the platform until the concrete strength, anchor type and edge distance are accepted. Do not load a bracket on concrete that has only been struck.
Changing from a ground-supported platform to a wall-anchored platform is a design change. Strike the old load path only under a permit to dismantle.
Keep the supplier’s coordinated drawings in the brief, and still have them checked under the project procedure. One supplier is not one design.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 30 September 2026 Coroner Megan Fairweather delivered findings, in chambers, into the death of Andrew Stephen Jones, 37. He died at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital at 2.19pm on 25 July 2021 from blunt force chest injuries after he was struck by a freestanding aluminium tower scaffold while watching his son play football at Mitchelton Football Club in Brisbane. The tower had been installed in April 2021 as a filming platform for matches. It stood in an open, publicly accessible area between two pitches and was expected to remain for several months. Scaffmag’s report of the findings, which links the coroner’s PDF, records an overall height of about 3.1 m, a working platform just over 2.1 m, a minimum base of 1.28 m and a height-to-base ratio of about 1.6:1. The coroner’s findings record the platform at 2145 mm above ground, on four swivel jacks on timber boards to suit a slight slope, and no outriggers. The inquest heard that this was inside the widely used guidance that a tower with a base greater than 1.2 m could be treated as stable where the working height did not exceed three times the minimum base dimension. The coroner found that relying on that ratio alone did not provide an adequate assessment of wind risk. Senior structural engineer Aaron Poole estimated a critical wind range for toppling of 47 to 54 km/h. Evidence before the inquest placed likely gusts on the day between 41 and 68 km/h. AS/NZS 4576:2020 advises that freestanding tower scaffolds should not be operated or left unattended where wind speeds may exceed 40 km/h. Queensland’s Scaffolding Code referred to “strong winds” without defining the term or giving installers a simple method for deciding when extra controls were required. Mr Poole’s evidence was that outriggers, tie-downs, tube-and-clip restraints and additional dead load could substantially increase stability, could withstand wind above 70 km/h, and would very likely have prevented the incident. Because the working platform was below four metres, erection did not require a Queensland High Risk Work Licence for scaffolding, routine inspections were not required, and there was no requirement for a formal handover certificate. The coroner found there had been no formal plan for ongoing monitoring after installation, and that the circumstances raised issues broader than the actions of any individual.

This is a Queensland coronial finding. It is not UK law, and it does not amend TG20, BS EN 12811-1 or the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The temporary works point travels. A low freestanding tower that satisfies a height-to-base rule of thumb can still be unstable in wind, particularly if it is unclad or sheeted, left unattended, standing for months, or placed where the public can be underneath or beside it. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. Consequence here was a member of the public, not an operative on the platform. On a UK site the same arrangement is a temporary works item: design or configure it, check it against the manufacturer’s instructions and the applicable TG20 compliance sheet, and manage it under the project temporary works procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for that procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. HSE’s scaffolding guidance expects scaffolds to be designed, erected, altered and dismantled by competent people, and inspected by a competent person before first use, after alteration, after an event that may have affected stability, and at intervals not exceeding seven days. A weather event is that kind of event. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. Public interface, duration and wind exposure can take a mobile tower out of a default low category.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put freestanding and mobile towers on the temporary works register, including towers hired for filming, inspection or short-duration access, and towers left standing between uses.

Do not treat a 3:1 height-to-base ratio as a wind design. Match the configuration to the manufacturer’s instructions and the TG20 sheet. If the sheet does not cover the height, the ties, the sheeting or the location, it is outside the sheet.
Brief wind, exposure, duration and public interface in the design brief. Outriggers, kentledge and ties are design controls, not site improvisation after the forecast arrives.

Set a weather trigger before erection: who checks the forecast, what wind speed stops use, and who has authority to dismantle, tie or exclude. AS/NZS 4576:2020’s 40 km/h figure is Australian guidance, not a UK limit. Use the manufacturer’s limit and the project procedure.
Where the public can reach the tower, exclusion and stability are both required. A tower between pitches, on a pavement or beside a site hoarding is a public-protection item.
Inspect before first use and after wind, alteration or a period left unattended. A tower below a licensing threshold in another jurisdiction is not outside inspection on a UK site.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 2 October 2026 the Health and Safety Executive published the sentencing of W G Carter Limited, of 81A Eaton Road, Appleton, Oxfordshire, after carpenter Richard “Felix” Roper died following a fall at Manor Barn House, Nether Westcote, Gloucestershire. On 30 August 2022 he was replacing damaged floor joists on the first floor while other workers removed sections of flooring in the same area. Extensive repairs were under way to rotten joists and floorboards. Large parts of the first-floor structure had been stripped, leaving open gaps between joists. Some joists were missing or had not been secured. He fell from the first floor to the concrete ground floor, sustained severe head injuries, and died in hospital the following day. A joint investigation by HSE and Gloucestershire Police found that the work at height had not been properly planned, appropriately supervised, or carried out safely. Workers, including Mr Roper, could reach areas where flooring and structural supports had been removed, and other workers were still removing floorboards, creating and increasing the fall risk. HSE served a Prohibition Notice stopping further work at height until adequate measures were introduced. On 24 September 2026 at Bristol Magistrates’ Court the company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. It was fined £120,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,247. HSE principal inspector James Lucas said a man lost his life because of the company’s failings, and that appropriate controls could have prevented the death.

A floor that is being opened up is not the permanent structure the operatives walked on at the start of the shift. Removing boards and joists changes the load path, the available standing area and the fall consequence. That is a temporary works condition, whether or not anyone has called it one. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require the work to be properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out in a manner which is, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe. HSE’s published guidance on falls from height says work must be planned, supervised and carried out by competent people. CDM 2015 still requires construction work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s temporary works guidance says any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand the foreseeable loads on it, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed. On a strip-out, the temporary structure may be a crash deck, a scaffold working platform, a designed temporary deck spanning sound joists, or a decision that nobody stands on the incomplete floor at all. BS 5975-1:2024 is the code of practice for the management procedure. It is not a statute and it does not appoint a person. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. Standard does not automatically mean low risk: a domestic barn conversion became fatal because the fall was onto concrete and the sequence was uncontrolled. Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Put floor strip-out, joist replacement and any temporary deck or crash deck on the temporary works register before the first board is lifted.
Do not allow people to work on a floor while other trades are still removing boards or joists in the same area. Sequence the opening, or exclude it.
Treat missing or unsecured joists as a failed working surface. Access needs a designed platform, work from below, or a physical barrier, not a verbal warning.
If a crash deck or temporary deck is the control, brief it, check it and permit it before use. A few loose boards laid back over the opening is not a deck.
Give the Temporary Works Coordinator authority to stop access to an incomplete floor. A domestic or small-works site is not outside the procedure.

After alteration, weather or a change of trade, re-inspect before anyone is allowed back on. The method used after this incident — joists installed from below, first floor closed to access — is the arrangement that should have been in the RAMS first.
Do not proceed until the arrangement has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: A return, a 1.5 m lift and a timber brace are temporary works — match the sheet to the wall
posts.excerpt: NASC’s TG20 ePortal update (4 September 2026), restated in Scaffolding Insider on 30 September, adds 1.5 m lifts and scaffold returns to tube-and-fitting compliance sheets. CROSS-UK Report 1525 (13 May 2026) describes ad hoc timber bracing to masonry with no design. posts.linkedinReady:
A compliance sheet that does not match the scaffold on the wall is not a compliance sheet. A timber brace leaned against a new masonry wall because “that is how we have always done it” is not a temporary works design.

Two UK publications, and one overseas fatality, land in the same place this week.

On 4 September 2026 NASC added two options to the TG20 ePortal for tube and fitting scaffolds: 1.5 m lift heights, and returns. The September Scaffolding Insider, published on 30 September, flags that update again. A 1.5 m lift is the height many bricklayers actually work to. A return is where the scaffold turns the corner. When a return is selected, the compliance sheet includes an extra page for internal and external returns: how far the scaffold extends, how it is connected, and how it is tied as it goes around the building. The new options currently apply to tube and fitting scaffolds in the TG20 version of the ePortal. If the sheet is still a straight run and the site has built a return, you are outside the sheet. The Temporary Works Coordinator should be checking the sheet against the elevation, not against last month’s template.

CROSS-UK Report 1525, published on 13 May 2026, is the other half of the same wall. The reporter describes ad hoc timber bracing to masonry with no design, no calculation and no oversight, and says principal contractors were not asking the TWC for a temporary works design inside the brickwork package. The Expert Panel is plain: a partially built wall can overturn under wind, impact or ordinary site activity. An improvised brace can add a hazard because nobody has checked how it works. Collapses of masonry walls during construction have historically caused serious injuries and fatalities. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure. CDM 2015 still requires the work to be planned, managed and monitored. HSE’s position has not moved: a temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained for the foreseeable loads on it, and used only for that purpose.

On 8 September 2026 in Bukit Mertajam, Penang, a worker died while dismantling scaffolding. Penang DOSH said he was on the eighth floor when the temporary catch platform supporting the scaffolding collapsed; he and the scaffold fell, and he suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. Work was stopped and the scene preserved. This is not a UK prosecution and the investigation is not finished. The control point travels. A catch platform, a fan or a crash deck is temporary works. Dismantling is a design case, not the reverse of erection done from memory.

Monday’s check:
- Put masonry stability and scaffold returns on the temporary works register before the bricklayers arrive.
- Match the TG20 compliance sheet to the lifts and returns that will actually be built. If the geometry is outside the sheet, it needs a design.
- Brief the dismantling sequence. A platform that carried the scaffold on the way up has to be checked for the way down.
- Give the TWC authority to stop informal bracing. A photo of a timber prop is not a permit.

body.p: On 4 September 2026 the National Access and Scaffolding Confederation published an update to TG20 in the ePortal. Users can select 1.5 m lift heights when configuring a tube and fitting scaffold, which NASC notes is particularly relevant to traditional new-build work where bricklayers need a suitable working height. The same update adds returns. When a return is selected, an additional page is included in the compliance sheet for internal and external returns, covering how far the scaffold should extend around the return, connection arrangements, and how the scaffold should be tied as it is returned around the building. NASC states that the new functionality is available in the TG20 version of the ePortal and currently applies to tube and fitting scaffolds. The September 2026 issue of Scaffolding Insider, announced on 30 September 2026, includes that TG20 update alongside the top-line messages from SG25 Access and Egress. The magazine announcement does not replace the compliance sheet: the sheet has to describe the scaffold that will be built.

body.h: CROSS 1525: bracing that was never designed
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1525, published on 13 May 2026, records a reporter’s concern about ad hoc timber bracing used to support masonry walls without a temporary works design, calculations or oversight. The reporter, who describes a life-changing injury from a masonry wall collapse during construction, says these makeshift systems are often poorly fixed and give a false sense of security. The reporter’s view is that principal contractors are not effectively communicating with Temporary Works Coordinators and are failing to identify or request a temporary works design within bricklayers’ work packages, leaving gaps against BS 5975-1:2024, CDM 2015 and the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The CROSS Expert Panel agrees that partially completed masonry walls can be vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads such as wind, impact or construction activities, and that collapses during construction have historically resulted in serious injuries and fatalities. The Panel notes that an improvised brace may be an attempt to address a known risk, but it may not provide reliable restraint and can introduce additional hazards because the behaviour of the system has not been assessed. The Panel points to BS 5975 as the management procedure and suggests simple best-practice solutions, possibly from the Temporary Works Forum, so that low-rise masonry does not depend on a bespoke design in every case or on an unassessed timber prop.

body.h: A catch platform is temporary works, including on the way down
body.p: On 10 September 2026 the New Straits Times reported a Penang Department of Occupational Safety and Health notification of a fatal accident at about 6.15 pm on 8 September 2026 at a construction site in Bukit Mertajam. DOSH said the worker was believed to have been dismantling scaffolding on the eighth floor when the temporary catch platform supporting the scaffolding structure collapsed. The worker and the scaffolding fell to a lower level; he suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene. Following preliminary investigations, Penang DOSH ordered the relevant work to stop and prohibited interference with the scene. DOSH reminded employers that work at height and scaffolding must be planned and carried out through risk assessment and controls, including safe access and egress and fall protection. This is an overseas notification, not a UK enforcement outcome, and the investigation had not been concluded in the report. It is included because the failed element was a temporary structure supporting scaffolding during dismantling, which is the same class of temporary works a UK contractor would be expected to identify, design or configure, and inspect.

HSE’s temporary works guidance says any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads imposed on it, and used only for the purpose for which it was designed, installed and maintained. HSE describes appointment of a Temporary Works Coordinator, with authority to stop unsatisfactory work, as an effective way of managing that duty. On a housing or low-rise site that means the brickwork package and the scaffold package both sit on the register: wall stability while the wall is incomplete, lift height and returns on the compliance sheet, and the catch platform or fan during erection and striking. If the scaffold geometry is inside the TG20 sheet, follow the sheet, including the return page. If it is not, it needs a design. Informal timber bracing should not be accepted as a substitute for either. Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

A board walkway in a live lane is not just traffic management. It is a temporary structure that the public will use without signing onto your site.

On 21 September 2026 the Department for Transport opened a consultation, with Transport Scotland, the Welsh Government and the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, on updating the Safety at Street Works and Road Works Code of Practice. The current code dates from 2013. The consultation runs until 14 December 2026. The draft is not yet the issued code.

What the draft is asking the industry to look at is familiar ground for a Temporary Works Coordinator: usable footway width when works occupy the pavement; a 1.0 m pinch limited to 6 m including any walkway in the carriageway; ramps, surfaces and barriers that actually separate people from traffic; a clearer hierarchy for cycle routes; and new language for hard and soft closures. Failure to comply with the issued code is already treated as evidence of failing the legal duty to sign, light and guard.

That duty does not wait for 14 December. CDM 2015 still requires you to protect people other than your employees. HSE still treats excavations, barriers, temporary slopes and site fencing as temporary works. BS 5975-1:2024 still puts public-interface items on the register, names a TWC, and requires a brief, inspection and permit before the public is invited onto a boarded walkway, a ramped crossing or a narrowed footway next to an open trench.

Do not treat Chapter 8 diagrams or a Red Book layout as a substitute for checking that the boards, props, ramps and barriers can take the load and will stay put overnight. Do not treat a consultation draft as a reason to drop the 2013 arrangements that are still in force.

body.p: On 21 September 2026 the Department for Transport published an open consultation on updating the Safety at Street Works and Road Works Code of Practice. The current code was last updated in 2013. The draft has been developed jointly with Transport Scotland, the Welsh Government and the Department for Infrastructure in Northern Ireland, with support from specialist consultants Arup AECOM and input from the Highway Authorities and Utilities Committee safety working group and other expert organisations including the Health and Safety Executive. The consultation opened on 21 September 2026 and closes on 14 December 2026. In England and Wales the issued code is statutory guidance under section 65 of the New Roads and Street Works Act 1991 and section 174 of the Highways Act 1980. The consultation page states that failure to comply with the code is evidence of failure to fulfil legal obligations to sign, light and guard works, and that compliance with the code will be taken as compliance with the legal requirements to which it relates. The code does not apply to motorways and high-speed dual carriageways of 50 miles per hour or more; Chapter 8 of the Traffic Signs Manual covers some of those situations.

The consultation document lists proposed changes including: maintaining safe and accessible pedestrian routes around works, including minimum footway widths, the length of restricted widths and improved standards for temporary walkways; managing cycle routes with a clearer hierarchy that prioritises keeping cyclists on their original route; introducing definitions of hard and soft road closures; strengthened requirements to support disabled people and other vulnerable road users; updated diagrams reflecting Traffic Signs Regulations and General Directions and Chapter 8; expanded guidance on mobile and short-duration works and working near level crossings and tramways; and language that distinguishes mandatory requirements from advisory guidance. On usable width, the consultation text states that where a pedestrian route is restricted to 1 metre, the draft code allows that restriction only for a maximum length of 6 metres, including temporary walkways in the carriageway. Pages 52 to 60 of the draft place greater emphasis on continuous temporary walkways with appropriate ramp gradients, smoother surfaces and barriers separating pedestrians from traffic. These are consultation proposals. They are not yet issued requirements.

Utility openings, highway repairs, boarded walkways, ramped crossings, barriers, temporary fencing, spoil next to a trench and plant sitting on a live footway are temporary works with a public interface. The people using that route did not attend your induction. CDM 2015 duties to persons other than employees sit alongside the issued street-works code and the project temporary works procedure. BS 5975-1:2024 still requires the item on the register, a competent Temporary Works Coordinator, a design brief when the walkway, barrier or excavation is not a documented standard arrangement for the actual geometry and loading, inspection before use, and a permit. A Chapter 8 or Red Book layout that has not been checked for the boards, supports, ramps and overnight condition is not a completed brief. The 2013 code remains the issued statutory guidance until a revised code is published. Do not implement draft-only dimensions as if they had already replaced the current code, and do not use the consultation as a reason to leave an occupied footway or an unsupported excavation without control.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register street-works walkways, ramps, barriers, fencing, excavations, spoil heaps and plant sitting next to an open trench.
Treat a boarded walkway in the carriageway as a temporary structure with a public live load, not only as traffic management.
Issue a design brief when the arrangement is not a documented standard solution for the actual width, span, ramp gradient, vehicle impact risk and overnight condition.
Keep spoil and plant far enough from the excavation edge that they do not surcharge the ground the public is walking beside.
Inspect before first use and after any alteration, vehicle strike or weather that could move boards, barriers or supports.
Do not open the route to the public until the project procedure has issued the permit.
Read the DfT consultation if you place or design street works. Respond by 14 December 2026 if you have evidence on widths, ramps or closures. Do not treat the draft as the issued code.
Provisional category only — confirm under the project temporary works procedure. Public interface and live traffic push the category up.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: Unsecured stairwell openings are temporary works, not leftover carpentry
posts.excerpt: HSE press release 21 September 2026: Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd was fined £300,000 plus £9,284.05 costs at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026 after labourer Joseph Tuck, 24, fell one storey through an unprotected stairwell opening in January 2024. Loose scaffold boards that had covered the void had been removed. Edges were unprotected. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and the HART team recovered him unconscious. Spinal injuries ended his return to physical work. HSE Inspector Louise Redgrove called it a wholly avoidable failure of planning and supervision. For contractors this is a floor-opening control item that belongs on the temporary works register.
posts.linkedinReady:
A stairwell without a staircase is not a finishing detail. It is an opening through a working floor, and it is temporary works until it is covered or guarded and inspected.

HSE published the outcome on 21 September 2026. Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd was found guilty on three charges at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026 and fined £300,000 plus £9,284.05 costs. In January 2024 Joseph Tuck, 24, in his second week as a temporary labourer for a scaffolding company on a four-house site, stepped backwards through a stairwell that had no staircase. Loose scaffold boards that had covered the void had been removed. Edges were unprotected. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and the HART team recovered him unconscious. Spinal injuries ended his return to physical work.

HSE Inspector Louise Redgrove said securing the boards or installing edge protection would have prevented the fall. Planning and supervision of work at height had failed.

That is the TWC and TWS point. Loose boards over a void are not a cover. Register every floor and stair opening. Specify a secured cover or guardrail. Inspect after boards are moved and before other trades walk the floor. Housing plots are not outside BS 5975-1:2024.

Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: The Health and Safety Executive published a prosecution release on 21 September 2026. Hillbeck Homes (Sowerby Bridge) Ltd, formerly of 1 Bretton Place, Otley Road, Guiseley, was found guilty on three charges at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 16 September 2026. The company was fined £300,000 and ordered to pay £9,284.05 in costs. In January 2024 Joseph Tuck, then 24 and in his second week as a temporary labourer for a scaffolding company, was working on a site of four new dwellings in Sowerby Bridge. He stepped backwards and fell one storey onto concrete through an opening intended for a staircase that had not yet been installed. The opening had not been securely covered. Previous loose scaffold boards had been removed. Open edges were not protected. There were no alternative means of accessing the sub-floor. West Yorkshire Fire & Rescue and the HART team rescued him after he fell unconscious. He sustained serious spinal injuries, was unable to work for months and has not returned to a physical job.

HSE found that Hillbeck Homes had failed to put adequate measures in place to prevent falls from height. The company failed to properly plan and appropriately supervise work at height and to take suitable and sufficient measures to prevent a fall. HSE Inspector Louise Redgrove stated that falls from height remain one of the leading causes of death in construction, accounting for around a quarter of all fatal injuries to workers each year, and that this incident was wholly avoidable. She stated that securing the scaffold boards or installing edge protection would have prevented the fall. HSE guidance cited in the release requires task-specific planning, risk assessment and physical safeguards such as scaffolding, guardrails or coverings where people may fall through openings in floors, roofs or other work platforms.

Housing plots still generate the same temporary works items as multi-storey frames: floor openings, incomplete stairs, scaffold-board covers, edge protection and access for following trades. A void that is convenient for the staircase gang is a fall-through hazard for every other person on that floor. Loose boards are a common site habit. They are not a designed cover, they are not inspected as temporary works and they can be lifted without a permit. The principal contractor retains the duty to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase under CDM 2015. Work at Height Regulations 2005 require suitable and sufficient measures to prevent a fall. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure that puts openings on the register, names a Temporary Works Coordinator and Temporary Works Supervisor, and requires inspection before use. Standard does not automatically mean low risk: a one-storey domestic opening has a high consequence if someone falls onto concrete.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every stair void, floor opening, service riser and roof light as a temporary works item from first cut until the permanent stair, cover or guard is complete and accepted.

Do not treat loose scaffold boards as a cover. A cover must be secured against displacement, capable of the imposed load, clearly marked and inspected. If boards are lifted for access, restore and inspect before other trades walk the floor.
Provide edge protection to open edges where a cover is not in place. Guardrails are not optional because the plot is domestic or the drop is only one storey.
Stop work and re-inspect after weekend stand-down, after following trades move boards, and after any change to access routes.
Confirm who is TWC and TWS for the housing package. Scaffold contractors covering voids still need the principal contractor’s procedure, brief and permit.
Task-specific risk assessment and RAMS must name the opening, the cover or guard detail, the inspection frequency and the rescue plan. A generic work-at-height paragraph is not enough.

Provisional design or check category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. A simple cover can escalate where public or occupied rooms sit below, or where debris and plant loads are applied.
Do not proceed until the opening control has been reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

Subject to project-specific verification of opening size, drop height, cover capacity, edge-protection arrangement, sequence and responsible persons, and to acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. Facts, dates, fines, names and inspector comments are taken from the HSE Media Centre release of 21 September 2026; confirm against that page before relying on them. posts.title: Late sequence changes and premature strut removal: temporary conditions that redesign the structure
posts.excerpt: CROSS 1479 (13 January 2026): contractor switched from paired beam lifts to single beams on a 20 m filler-beam bridge deck, introducing lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete (utilisation >200 %). CROSS 1388 (26 August 2025): one raking strut removed from a pipe-pile retaining wall because it obstructed the transfer slab, leaving an unsafe temporary condition. Network Rail EAN03/2025 (September 2025) now defines and requires consideration of temporary conditions. Both cases show the same control gap: sequence or site decisions that alter the assumed temporary state without TWC coordination, re-assessment or independent check.
posts.linkedinReady:
A late change to the lift sequence or the quiet removal of one raking strut is not a programme tweak. It is a temporary condition that can turn a designed structure into an unstable one.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1479 (13 January 2026) records a near-miss on an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Shortly before Category II check the contractor switched from lifting connected beam pairs to lifting single beams. The change introduced lateral-torsional buckling risk under the wet concrete load. Unrestrained, utilisation exceeded 200 %. The permanent-works designer flagged the need for temporary LTB restraints; the contractor initially declined, then challenged the bracing again two weeks before the pour. Bracing was finally designed and installed under severe time pressure with reinforcement already fixed. Independent checking caught the issue. Network Rail subsequently issued Engineering Advice Note EAN03/2025, *A consideration of temporary conditions* (September 2025), precisely because temporary states had been under-considered.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1388 (26 August 2025) is the complementary failure mode. A retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was holding a slope until the transfer slab could be cast. One strut obstructed the slab work, so it was removed. An unsafe length of temporary works was created. The Expert Panel is clear: any change (authorised or not) must be agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor; the Temporary Works Coordinator must be consulted; daily coordination meetings exist to surface exactly these clashes before an operative acts.

Both reports sit inside the same control gap. The permanent works are designed for the finished state. The temporary condition is created on site by sequence change, late commercial pressure or simple obstruction. Without a named TWC who has authority, a live register, a clear brief and a permit system, the load path and the stability assumptions disappear.

For the TWC and TWS this week:

- Treat any alteration to lift sequence, prop layout or construction order as a design change that requires re-assessment and independent check before it is executed.
- Do not accept “we will sort the bracing later” or “just take that strut out for an hour”.
- Confirm that temporary lateral-torsional restraint, plan bracing and end rotational restraint are present before wet concrete or other construction loads are applied to single beams.
- Keep the temporary-works register current with every sequence change; the register is not a filing exercise.
- On rail or highway interfaces, read Network Rail EAN03/2025 and the updated Health & Safety by Design guidance on temporary conditions.
- Independent check category remains provisional until confirmed under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Safety Report 1479 was published on 13 January 2026. During the final stages of design for an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck, shortly before Category II check, the contractor altered the intended construction sequence. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (with precast concrete infill providing temporary stability), the beams were to be lifted individually. The change introduced a significant temporary stability concern: lateral-torsional buckling of the beams under the weight of the wet concrete. The Category II checker identified that unbraced single beams without rotational restraint at the flange ends could experience buckling under a utilisation factor of over 200 %. The permanent-works designer confirmed the assessment and notified the contractor that temporary LTB restraints were required. The contractor initially declined an offer for the permanent-works designer to design the bracing, insisting on its own temporary-works team. Approximately three months later, and only two weeks before the deck concrete pour, the contractor again challenged the need for bracing. Final bracing was designed under compressed programme, with most deck reinforcement already fixed, restricting installation space. The event was classified as a near-miss. Independent checking prevented failure.

body.h: What the Expert Panel added on 1479
body.p: The CROSS Expert Panel notes that single beams are especially vulnerable to lateral-torsional buckling during lifting and under wet concrete, particularly where load reversal can occur. Simply providing cross-bracing between pairs is generally insufficient; plan bracing is needed to prevent both beams buckling together. The role of the Temporary Works Coordinator appears to have been under-delivered: clarity of design responsibility for temporary conditions was lacking. Communication of the need for temporary bracing was not demonstrably understood. Network Rail subsequently produced a definition of temporary conditions and published Engineering Advice Note EAN03/2025, *A consideration of temporary conditions* (September 2025). The Panel emphasises that permanent-works and temporary-works designers depend on each other and must exchange information openly.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1388 was published on 26 August 2025. A retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was containing a slope until a transfer slab could be constructed. One of the raking struts obstructed the contractor’s work on the slab and was removed, creating an unsafe section of temporary works. The resident engineer instructed remedial works and required the transfer slab to be completed and the wall stabilised before controlled prop removal. The Expert Panel states that there have been numerous failures resulting from changes (authorised or otherwise) to temporary and permanent works, often with unforeseen consequences. Any proposed change must be agreed with both the principal designer and the principal contractor. If a Temporary Works Coordinator is present, that person must be consulted. The contractor is responsible for the temporary works and should have understood the reason the strut was there. Daily coordination meetings are the normal place to surface such clashes before an operative acts.

Network Rail Engineering Advice Note EAN03/2025, issue 1, *A consideration of temporary conditions*, was published in September 2025 and is referenced in the updated Health & Safety by Design guidance on early focus on constructability and temporary works (Issue 4.1, September 2025). It defines temporary conditions as interim states that occur during alteration of existing assets or construction of new assets prior to completion of the permanent works. Not every temporary condition requires formal temporary works, but all temporary conditions must be considered in design risk assessment and coordinated between permanent-works and temporary-works designers. The guidance replaces earlier advice and aligns with BS 5975-1:2024 and BS 5975-2:2024.

Both reports describe decisions made on site or late in the design programme that altered the assumed temporary state of the structure. In one case the lift sequence was changed for commercial and programme reasons; in the other a single prop was removed to clear a work face. In neither case was the temporary condition re-assessed through the formal temporary-works procedure before the change was executed. The permanent works were designed for the finished state. The temporary condition is created by the sequence, the plant, the props that are present or absent, and the loads that are applied before the permanent restraints exist. CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024 require a named Temporary Works Coordinator, a register, a brief, design and check, inspection and permit. A verbal instruction or an unrecorded site decision is not those controls.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register any proposed change to lift sequence, beam connection status, prop layout or construction order as a temporary-works design change before it is executed.
Do not accept single-beam lifting or unrestrained beams under wet concrete without temporary lateral-torsional restraint, plan bracing and end rotational restraint verified by design and check.
Treat premature or unplanned removal of any temporary prop, strut or brace as a red-card event that requires immediate stop, re-assessment and formal permit before work continues.
Confirm that the Temporary Works Coordinator has been consulted and that the change has been agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor.
Keep the temporary-works register live; sequence changes must appear on it with the revised design status and check category.
On rail or highway interfaces, obtain and apply Network Rail EAN03/2025 and the current Health & Safety by Design temporary-conditions guidance.

Independent check category is provisional only and must be confirmed under the project temporary works procedure. Single beams under construction loads and retaining walls with incomplete propping are not default CAT 0 items.
Use daily coordination meetings to surface spatial clashes between temporary works and follow-on activities before operatives act.

posts.title: The prop can take the load. The slab, the sequence and the strut that was moved may not.
posts.excerpt: CROSS 1539 (14 May 2026): props sized for the column load, existing RC slab and beam not checked for the new load path. CROSS 1479 (13 January 2026): a late change from paired beam lifts to single lifts introduced lateral-torsional buckling under wet concrete. CROSS 1388 (26 August 2025): a raking strut removed because it obstructed a slab pour. HSE still requires temporary support in alteration and demolition to be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads. A mid-September 2026 RIDDOR consultation would widen reportable falling-object events on demolition and construction.
posts.linkedinReady:
A prop that can take the force is not the same thing as a safe temporary works scheme.

CROSS-UK Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, is the load-path case. A reporter was asked to advise on temporary works so a defective reinforced concrete column at the base of a multi-storey block of flats could be replaced with steel. Characteristic load on the column was estimated at over 1,165 kN, design load about 1,590 kN. The proposed props could carry those forces. There was no evidence the prop designer had checked the existing slab and beams that would transfer load into the column above. Once that check was done, the existing members were not strong enough in bending and shear. The reporter's view is blunt: it is not acceptable to issue a temporary works drawing without checking the existing structure, caveats included. Without the more complex scheme and method statement that followed, removing the column would have put a significant part of the building at risk of collapse.

CROSS-UK Report 1479, published 13 January 2026, is the sequence-change case. On an approximately 20 m filler-beam bridge deck, shortly before the Category II check finished, the contractor changed from lifting steel beams in connected pairs to lifting them one at a time. Unbraced single beams under wet concrete were assessed at over 200 percent utilisation in lateral-torsional buckling. Pair bracing alone is not enough if both beams can buckle together; plan restraint and end rotational restraint matter. Network Rail published B&S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025 in September 2025 on temporary conditions after reviews of this type of risk.

CROSS-UK Report 1388, published 26 August 2025, is the premature-removal case. A 600 mm pipe-pile wall with raking props was holding a slope until a transfer slab was built. One strut was in the way of the slab works and was taken out. That left a section of temporary works unsafe. CROSS learning: any change to the approved arrangement needs the principal designer and principal contractor, and a Temporary Works Coordinator who can stop the sequence until a revised scheme is agreed.

HSE's page on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling is the same duty in regulator language. Temporary support must be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads. A competent person decides the method. Supports are inspected and dismantled to the designer specification. The mid-September 2026 RIDDOR consultation, reported on 14 September 2026, proposes adding more falling-object events from buildings or structures under demolition or construction to the reportable list. That does not change the control. It would widen what has to be reported if the control fails.

For the TWC and TWS this week:

Do not accept a prop schedule that only proves the prop. Demand the load path through existing slabs, beams, walls and foundations.
Treat a change of lift sequence, pour sequence or prop layout as a design change, not a site convenience.
Do not remove a strut, tie or brace because it is in the way until a revised scheme and permit are in place.
Independent check category is provisional only, to be confirmed under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: CROSS-UK Safety Report 1539 was published on 14 May 2026. A reporter was asked to advise on temporary works to allow removal of a defective reinforced concrete column and replacement with a new steel column. The column sat at the base of a multi-storey block of flats. Estimated characteristic load exceeded 1,165 kN; estimated design load was approximately 1,590 kN. The proposed props could take the required forces. The reporter found no evidence that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Analysis of the existing beams and slabs showed they were not strong enough to transfer load from the temporary props to the concrete column above and would fail in bending and shear. The reporter states it is unacceptable to issue what is effectively a temporary works drawing without checking the existing structure, irrespective of caveats on the drawing. A more complex temporary works system and a written method statement were then prepared. CROSS records that the contractor could have removed the defective column without those additional works, in which case a significant part of the building would likely have collapsed.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1479 was published on 13 January 2026. During the final stages of design of an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck, shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor altered the intended construction sequence. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs, beams were to be lifted individually. That change introduced a temporary stability concern: lateral-torsional buckling of the beams under the weight of wet concrete. Assessment indicated that main beams left unbraced and without rotational restraint at the flange ends could see a utilisation factor of over 200 percent. The designer confirmed the assessment and told the contractor that temporary lateral-torsional buckling restraints were required. CROSS notes that simply providing cross-bracing between pairs of beams is not generally sufficient; plan bracing is needed to prevent both beams buckling together. Following review of temporary conditions of this type, Network Rail published B&S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025, A consideration of temporary conditions, in September 2025.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1388 was published on 26 August 2025. A retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props contained a slope until a transfer slab could be built. One raking strut obstructed slab works and was removed, leaving a section of the temporary works unsafe. The reporter instructed remedial works and required the transfer slab to be completed and the wall stabilised before props were removed in a controlled sequence. CROSS-UK Safety Report 1486, published 20 November 2025, records a partial collapse overnight during underpinning. Before the underpinning, portions of intermediate internal floors and walls had been removed to create workspace. Those removals destabilised the building. CROSS learning outcomes include appointing a competent Temporary Works Coordinator in accordance with BS 5975-1:2024 and not removing structural elements before the designer has confirmed that the temporary works plan accounts for that state. CROSS notes that, from the limited information, the event may well have justified HSE enforcement including a prohibition notice until the site was made safe.

body.h: HSE duty and the September 2026 RIDDOR consultation
body.p: HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that a competent person should decide the method and design of temporary supports. Temporary support must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads. Structures should never be overloaded. Bracing and propping should be designed by experienced temporary works designers and installed, checked, inspected, maintained and dismantled in accordance with the designer specification. Demolition or dismantling arrangements should be written down before work begins. On 14 September 2026 The Scotsman reported HSE consultation on a major review of RIDDOR. Proposed additions on dangerous occurrences include situations where an object falls from a building or structure under demolition or construction where it could cause death. Reforms, if made, are described as unlikely to take effect before 2028. The consultation does not alter the existing CDM duty to control temporary works; it would widen what is reportable if control fails.

These reports sit in different packages: column replacement in an occupied block, a short-span bridge deck, a piled retaining wall, underpinning. The control gap is the same. The item that looks designed is only part of the scheme. The existing structure that receives the prop load is not checked. The lift or pour sequence changes after the Category II check is nearly finished. A strut is removed because it is in the way. Floors and walls come out to make space before the temporary works plan has a stable load path for the remaining building. CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024 require a named coordinator, a register, a brief that includes existing structure and sequence, design and check, inspection and permit. A prop table and a verbal agreement to move a strut are not those controls.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Do not accept a propping drawing that only proves the prop capacity. Require the load path through existing slabs, beams, walls, columns and foundations, with condition survey where the structure is existing.
Treat a change from paired lifts to single lifts, or any other change to erection or pour sequence, as a design change that restarts briefing and check, not as a site instruction.
Do not remove a raking strut, tie, brace or prop because it obstructs the next activity until a revised scheme is designed, checked and permitted.
Do not strip intermediate floors or walls to create workspace until the temporary works designer has confirmed stability of the remaining structure, including out-of-hours and weather cases.
On filler-beam and similar decks, check lateral-torsional buckling of single members under wet concrete and construction load. Pair bracing is not automatically plan restraint.
Keep the Temporary Works Coordinator in the conversation between permanent works designer, temporary works designer and the package that wants the sequence changed.

Independent check category is provisional only and must be confirmed under the project temporary works procedure. Column replacement in an occupied multi-storey building and unbraced bridge beams under wet concrete are not default CAT 0 items.
Write demolition, alteration and dismantling sequences down before work starts. Inspect supports to the designer specification, not to a general scaffold ticket.

Subject to project-specific verification of existing structure capacity, condition, load path, construction sequence, bracing, weather, occupancy and responsible persons, and to acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. Loads, utilisation figures, dates and CROSS report IDs are taken from the cited CROSS and HSE pages as published; confirm against the original notices before relying on them. Exact clause references in BS 5975-1:2024, CDM 2015, BS EN 1991-1-6, Network Rail EAN03/2025 and HSE guidance are to be confirmed against the project licensed copy. posts.title: Ad hoc masonry braces and crane-base examples: two places procedure still fails
posts.excerpt: CROSS 1525 (13 May 2026, recirculated by CROSS on X in August): ad hoc timber bracing to masonry walls without design, calculation or TWC oversight. CROSS 1552 (29 June 2026): a CIRIA C761 worked example used for shear enhancement on a square piled tower-crane base where the panel says enhancement should not be used in the uplift case. HSE Poole blockwork-wall prosecution remains the enforcement reminder that a wall without a temporary works design is still temporary works.
posts.linkedinReady:
A length of timber nailed to a half-built wall is not a temporary works design. Neither is copying a worked example past the load case it was written for.

CROSS Safety Report 1525, published 13 May 2026 and still being circulated by CROSS in August, records a reporter concern that masonry walls on site are still being held up with ad hoc timber bracing. No design. No calculations. No Temporary Works Coordinator oversight. The reporter describes a life-changing injury from a masonry wall that collapsed during construction. The Expert Panel is clear: partially completed masonry is vulnerable to overturning from modest wind, impact or construction activity. Improvised restraint can add hazards the site team has not assessed. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management procedure they point to. The Panel also asks industry bodies, including the Temporary Works Forum, to consider simple standard solutions so low-rise masonry packages are not left as informal site practice.

CROSS Safety Report 1552, published 29 June 2026, is a different failure mode: guidance used beyond its limit. A reporter queried a worked example in CIRIA C761 Tower crane foundation and tie design. Shear enhancement was applied on a square piled crane base in a condition where overturning puts piles into tension. The CROSS panel generally agreed that shear enhancement should not be relied on when both the crane leg and the pile are in tension, because no compression strut can form. Design the base for the full shear demand without enhancement, and treat a published example as a teaching aid, not a project certificate.

HSE prosecution of Matrod Frampton Limited after a blockwork wall collapsed into an excavation at Poole on 19 August 2022 is the same lesson in court form. The wall was backfilled before the mortar had set. There was no temporary works design for the wall, no Temporary Works Coordinator and no Temporary Works Supervisor, despite a safety report eight days earlier. The company pleaded guilty. The court outcome was published in December 2025.

For the TWC and TWS this week:

Register free-standing and incomplete masonry as temporary works in the brickwork package, not after the first lift is standing.
Do not accept nailed timber as a designed brace unless it is a documented standard solution used inside its stated limits.
Inspect after wind, after weekend stand-down and after any change to wall height or opening.
On tower-crane bases, check the uplift and tension-pile cases separately. Do not import shear enhancement from a worked example without reading the load path.

body.p: CROSS-UK Safety Report 1525 was published on 13 May 2026. A reporter is concerned that ad hoc timber bracing is still used on sites to support masonry walls that do not have a temporary works design, calculations or oversight. The reporter states they suffered a life-changing injury when a masonry wall collapsed during construction. They describe makeshift systems that are poorly fixed and give a false sense of security. They attribute the gap to principal contractors not identifying temporary stability inside bricklayers work packages and not engaging the Temporary Works Coordinator before installation. CROSS cites BS 5975-1:2024, CDM 2015 and the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 as the compliance frame. CROSS recirculated the report on its official X account on 13 August 2026.

The CROSS Expert Panel treats temporary stability of masonry during construction as a well recognised safety concern. Partially completed walls can overturn under relatively modest wind, impact or construction loads. Collapses have historically caused serious injuries and fatalities. Ad hoc bracing may be an attempt to manage that risk, but it is not a reliable restraint and can introduce unassessed hazards. The Panel notes that low-rise masonry packages are often less controlled than other structural activities, leaving gaps in responsibility for both temporary and permanent stability. It asks industry bodies, including the Temporary Works Forum, to consider simple best-practice bracing solutions that do not require a bespoke design on every house plot.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1552 was published on 29 June 2026. A reporter is concerned that a worked example in CIRIA C761 Tower crane foundation and tie design applies shear enhancement in circumstances that may not be appropriate, particularly when overturning produces tension in the piles on one side of a square piled crane base. The reporter view is that shear enhancement should only be used where a compression load acts through the concrete so that part of the force can strut directly into the pile. Members of the CROSS panel generally agreed that shear enhancement cannot be applied in that worked-example condition when both the crane leg and the pile are in tension, because no compression strut can form on the detailing shown. The panel practical steer is to design the base for the full shear demand without enhancement, and not to treat a published example as covering every load case on the project.

On 19 August 2022 a newly built blockwork wall collapsed at a site on Old Coast Guard Road, Poole, crushing steel-fixer Patrick Grant, then 69, against the floor of an excavation. Construction Index reported the court outcome on 17 December 2025. Matrod Frampton Limited pleaded guilty at Bristol Magistrates Court. HSE found no temporary works design for the wall or for other temporary works on the site, and no Temporary Works Coordinator or Temporary Works Supervisor, despite a safety report eight days before the incident. Groundworkers backfilled the wall before the mortar had set. The company was fined 100000 pounds. The published HSE point is that design and execution of temporary works is a fundamental control, not an optional extra once the wall is standing.

CROSS-UK Newsletter 82 was issued on 3 September 2026. It collects the latest fire and structural safety reports. Contractors who only read enforcement notices will miss the near-miss pattern that CROSS exists to share. CIRIA C761 remains current as the UK tower-crane foundation and tie design guide. Neither document is a project design.

These records sit in different packages: brickwork, crane bases, excavations. The control gap is the same. Temporary stability is not identified early, the item is not registered, a standard or example is used outside its limit, and the TWC is asked after the risk is already on the wall or in the ground. CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024 require a named coordinator, a register, a brief, design and check, inspection and permit. A timber stay and a copied calculation sheet are not those controls.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Identify incomplete masonry, free-standing walls and unrestrained gables on the temporary works register before the first lift, inside the masonry work package.
Do not treat ad hoc nailed timber as an approved brace unless it is a documented standard solution used inside stated height, wind and opening limits.
Inspect masonry restraint after wind events, weekend stand-down, increase in wall height and formation of openings.
Keep people and plant out of the fall zone of an unrestrained wall. Do not backfill against green masonry.
On piled or pad crane bases, run the overturning and tension-pile cases as separate checks. Do not apply shear enhancement from CIRIA C761 examples to a tension interface.
Treat a published worked example as guidance. Confirm geometry, reinforcement, pile layout and load combination against the project design.
Appoint a Temporary Works Coordinator with authority to stop loading or backfilling. A safety report that names the gap and is then ignored is evidence, not a control.

body.h: The load path through the existing structure
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, describes a column replacement at the base of a multi-storey block of flats. The existing column carried an estimated characteristic load of over 1165 kN and an estimated design load of about 1590 kN. Proposed props were capable of taking the required forces. The reporter found no evidence that the prop designer had checked the existing RC slabs and beams that would transfer load from the props. Once that check was done, those members were not strong enough in bending and shear. The reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and a written method statement. Issuing a temporary works drawing without checking the existing structure is not acceptable, regardless of drawing caveats.

CROSS Safety Report 1479, published 13 January 2026, covers an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor altered the intended sequence from lifting steel beams in connected pairs to lifting them individually. That change introduced a temporary lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete. The Category II checker identified the unbraced individual beams as critical. Without rotational restraint at the flange ends, utilisation was reported as over 200 percent. The designer confirmed that temporary LTB restraints were required. CROSS highlights communication between the permanent works designer, the temporary works designer and the Temporary Works Coordinator, and points to Network Rail B and S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025 on temporary conditions (September 2025).

These three records are not the same site. They are the same management gap. A working platform used to store demolition arisings is temporary works. A prop that sits on an existing slab is temporary works that includes the slab. A lift or pour sequence that differs from the design assumption is a new temporary condition. CDM 2015, HSE temporary works and structural-stability pages, and BS 5975-1:2024 all point to the same controls: appoint a TWC with authority, register the item, write a brief, design and check, inspect, permit to load, and treat change as change.

ul: Register every working platform, debris deck, crash deck and floor used as a temporary store. State the intended debris or plant load in the brief.
Do not load a platform or prop without a design, an agreed check category and a permit-to-load signed by a competent person who has seen the as-built arrangement.
Close the load path through existing slabs, beams, walls, columns and foundations. A prop capacity check that stops at the head of the prop is incomplete.
Treat a change of erection sequence, lift pairing, pour bay or striking order as a design change. Re-brief, re-check, update the method and re-issue the permit.
Keep exclusion zones under loaded temporary platforms. Two trades stacked vertically need a written arrangement.
Inspect after debris is placed, after rainfall, and after any alteration to the platform or support.
Hold permit-to-strike until the permanent works can take the load.

Independent check category is provisional only. Platforms carrying unknown debris, props on existing structure of unknown capacity, and sequence changes on bridge decks normally point to escalation, not a CAT 0 close-out.
