body.p: The Temporary Works Forum held its 67th quarterly meeting at the Institution of Civil Engineers, One Great George Street, on Wednesday 9 September 2026. TWf's public meeting note records that Rob Millard opened the session, nine new member organisations had joined since the June meeting, and Andrew Jones of RMD Kwikform presented Calibrating CIRIA Report 108 for the Current Age. CIRIA 108 gives Pmax as the lesser of a rate-of-rise expression and full hydrostatic head. posts.title: Crane bases, AI-looking calculations and a missing temporary works procedure
posts.excerpt: This week's contractor briefing is about three control failures that still look respectable on paper: copying a CIRIA crane-base worked example without checking the tension-side shear case; accepting a polished calculation pack that was not a competent structural check; and running a site with no temporary works procedure, no Temporary Works Coordinator and no design for a wall that later collapsed into an excavation.
posts.linkedinReady:
A tower-crane base, a plant pad on an existing roof and a newly built blockwork wall next to an excavation are all temporary works. They need a brief, a competent design or accepted standard solution, a check that matches the actual load path, and a named Temporary Works Coordinator. Paper that looks finished is not the same as a structure that will stand.

Three published strands are worth putting in front of every TWC, TWS and commercial manager this week.

CROSS Report 1552 (29 June 2026) concerns Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761, Tower crane foundation and tie design. The reporter questioned whether shear enhancement used in that example is valid on the side of a square piled crane base where overturning puts the crane leg and pile into tension. The Expert Panel generally agreed: without a compression strut, shear enhancement should not be relied on for the uplift case. Design for the full shear demand, or use a strut-and-tie model with detailing that can actually be fixed. Do not copy a worked example or a spreadsheet derived from it and assume the geometry and load path on your site are the same.

CROSS Report 1554 (16 July 2026) is about heavy plant proposed on an existing flat-slab roof. An architect submitted a detailed-looking calculation pack to justify the extra load. A reviewing structural engineer found the roof was only suitable for light plant, that the technical content was wrong, and that the pack had the hallmarks of unverified AI output - including new errors after a rapid rewrite. The Expert Panel point is blunt: AI is not a substitute for competent structural judgement. Dutyholders must stay inside their competence. Existing-structure capacity is part of the temporary works load path whenever plant, a crane or a grillage is added.

HSE December 2025 prosecution of Matrod Frampton Ltd is the procedure case. A blockwork wall at a Poole site was backfilled before the mortar had set and collapsed into an excavation, causing life-changing injuries to a steel-fixer. There was no temporary works design for the wall or for other temporary works on the site, no Temporary Works Coordinator and no Temporary Works Supervisor, even though the company's own safety consultants had flagged the gap eight days earlier. The company was fined 100000 pounds plus costs for CDM 2015 Regulations 13(1) and 19(1).

What a competent TWC should do with this:

- Treat every tower-crane base, tie, climbing frame and chocking arrangement as a bespoke temporary works item. Check tension-side shear and do not treat CIRIA C761 examples as a calculation.
- Do not accept plant, grillage or crane loads on existing fabric without a competent existing-structure assessment. A well-written PDF is not a check.
- If there is no live temporary works procedure, no named TWC and no design for walls, excavations or backfill sequence, stop that item until the project procedure says it can proceed.

body.h: CROSS 1552 - CIRIA C761 worked examples are not a crane-base design
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1552 (published 29 June 2026) concerns Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761, Guide to tower crane foundation and tie design. The reporter had used the example and later questioned the shear check on a square piled crane base. The example applies shear enhancement on the compression side of the base. The reporter observed that the corresponding planes on the tension side - where overturning puts the crane leg and pile reaction into tension - were not checked in the same way, and that a compression strut cannot form if both reactions are in tension. The reporter own review indicated that tension-side shear adjacent to the pile could be substantially over-utilised if enhancement is stripped out. The Expert Panel generally agreed that shear enhancement cannot be applied in that worked-example detailing when both the crane leg and the pile are in tension. A simplified approach is to design the base for the full shear demand without enhancement; alternatively a strut-and-tie analysis can be used if the detailing can be fixed on site. The Panel also warned against standardising crane-base design through spreadsheets copied from guidance examples. Crane foundations are normally single, safety-critical, project-specific elements.

body.h: CROSS 1554 - polished calculations are not a competent check of existing fabric
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1554 (published 16 July 2026) describes a proposal to put heavy plant on the roof of a reinforced-concrete flat-slab building of fewer than seven storeys, with retail at ground floor and residential above. An architect issued a calculation report that looked detailed and included analysis figures. The reviewing structural engineer found the roof capable of supporting only light plant, existing ducts already on a steel grillage, and technical content that was factually wrong. The reporter concluded the pack was largely AI-generated, noting how quickly it was rewritten and that new errors appeared in later revisions. The Expert Panel stated that current AI systems are not known to be capable of structural engineering judgement, that LLM outputs can look authoritative while being wrong, and that checking and approval must remain with a suitably qualified and experienced structural engineer. Competence duties under Part 2A of the Building Regulations 2010 (Regulations 11F-11H) require dutyholders to stay within their expertise. For a Temporary Works Coordinator the lesson is the same as CROSS 1539: existing structure is part of the load path. Plant pads, grillages and crane bases that sit on existing fabric need an existing-structure assessment, not a well-presented file.

body.h: HSE Matrod Frampton - no procedure, no TWC, wall into an excavation
body.p: On 19 August 2022 at Old Coast Guard Road, Poole, a newly built breeze-block wall was backfilled before the mortar had set and collapsed into an excavation, crushing steel-fixer Patrick Grant against the concrete floor and causing life-changing injuries. HSE found no temporary works design for the wall or for other temporary works on the site, and no Temporary Works Coordinator or Temporary Works Supervisor, despite a safety report raising that concern eight days earlier. Without a temporary works procedure, groundworkers backfilled prematurely. Rescue was delayed by the absence of an emergency rescue plan and by use of an unstable ladder into a deep excavation. Matrod Frampton Ltd pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulations 13(1) and 19(1) and was fined 100000 pounds plus 8242 pounds costs and a 2000 pound victim surcharge at Bristol Magistrates Court on 5 December 2025. HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said a temporary works procedure should have been implemented as a matter of course and that the event was wholly avoidable.

body.h: What this means on a live register this week
body.p: Put tower-crane bases, ties, climbing frames and chocking on the Temporary Works Register as bespoke items. Require the designer to show the tension-side shear case and to state whether shear enhancement has been used and why it is valid for that geometry. Treat any proposal to place plant, a grillage or a crane on existing fabric as an existing-structure temporary works problem: demand drawings, a competent assessment and a check category under the project procedure. Confirm that walls next to excavations, backfill sequence and mortar cure are designed or covered by an accepted standard solution with hold points - they are temporary works, not a groundworks habit. If the project still has no named Temporary Works Coordinator and no written procedure, that is the first hold point. posts.title: Temporary works is still a structure: missing design, un-checked existing fabric, and late sequence changes
posts.excerpt: Recent HSE prosecutions and CROSS reports keep pointing to the same control gaps. Temporary platforms used without design or calculated capacity; propping schemes that never checked the existing slab and beam; late changes to construction sequence that introduced lateral-torsional buckling risk. Process, competence and load path — not exotic technology — remain the difference between a near-miss and a collapse.
posts.linkedinReady:
A temporary platform, a prop, a bracing frame or a single steel beam in a temporary condition is still a structure. It has a load path, a capacity and failure modes. When those are not designed, not checked against the existing fabric, or not re-checked after a sequence change, the result is predictable.

Three recent strands of material make the same point for contractors and Temporary Works Coordinators.

HSE’s June 2026 prosecution of the Paxton House platform collapse showed temporary wooden platforms used to collect concrete cores and debris with no design and no calculated safe load. An inspection form was completed, but not by a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to “clear and not overload” existed without a known capacity or monitoring. The platform collapsed onto a drilling operative working beneath it; he sustained life-changing injuries. Roots Contractors Ltd and Diacutt Ltd were fined for CDM 2015 breaches. HSE’s own guidance is clear: temporary structures must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads and inspected by a competent person.

CROSS Report 1539 (May 2026) described temporary propping that could take the required forces — but the designer had not checked the existing reinforced-concrete slab and beam that were to transfer those forces. Opening-up works later showed the existing members would have failed in bending and shear. The reporter had to redesign a more complex temporary works scheme and method statement. Without that intervention a significant part of the building was at risk of collapse. The Expert Panel noted a failure of the temporary works procedure that should have required a Temporary Works Coordinator and proportionate checking on a significant structure.

CROSS Report 1479 (January 2026) recorded a near-miss on a filler-beam bridge deck. Late in design the contractor changed the lifting sequence from braced pairs to individual beams. The Category II checker identified lateral-torsional buckling utilisation above 200 % under wet concrete. Temporary restraints were eventually provided, but only after compressed design time and with reinforcement already fixed, complicating installation. Network Rail has since published engineering advice on temporary conditions. The lesson is communication of sequence changes and explicit treatment of temporary stability between permanent and temporary works teams.

These are not exotic risks. They are process failures that BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 are written to close:

• Put every temporary platform, prop scheme, bracing system or temporary condition of permanent works on the Temporary Works Register.
• Require design (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity) and a calculated safe load before use.
• Check the existing structure that receives temporary loads — capacity, reinforcement, load path — before relying on it.
• Treat any change to construction sequence that affects temporary stability as a design change that needs Temporary Works Coordinator involvement and, where necessary, re-check.
• Ensure the person completing inspections or authorising a permit is competent for that class of temporary works.

body.h: HSE Paxton House — platform without design or calculated capacity
body.p: On 23 February 2024 at Paxton House in the City of London, temporary wooden platforms were erected under openings being cut through concrete floors to collect 16 kg cores and debris. A drilling operative working directly beneath one platform was struck when it collapsed under accumulated load. He sustained fractures to the neck and back and a bleed on the brain and has not returned to construction work. HSE’s investigation, published with the June 2026 prosecution, found no design for the platforms, no calculation of safe loading level, an inspection form completed by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator, and only verbal instructions to clear debris without a known capacity or effective monitoring. Roots Contractors Ltd (principal contractor) was fined £19,333 plus costs for breaching CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2). Diacutt Ltd was fined £13,000 plus costs for Regulation 15(2).

body.h: CROSS 1539 — temporary props that never checked the existing structure
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1539 (published 14 May 2026) concerned temporary propping to allow replacement of a defective column. The proposed props were capable of taking the required forces, yet no evidence was found that the temporary works designer had checked the existing reinforced-concrete slab and beam that were to transfer those loads. Opening-up works commissioned by the reporter revealed that the existing members were inadequate in bending and shear. The reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and method statement; without it a significant part of the building was at risk of collapse. The Expert Panel characterised the event as a failure of the temporary works procedure that should have included Temporary Works Coordinator oversight and proportionate checking on a significant structure.

body.h: CROSS 1479 — late sequence change and temporary lateral-torsional buckling risk
body.p: CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) described an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Shortly before Category II check completion the contractor altered the intended construction sequence from lifting steel beams in connected pairs to lifting them individually. The change introduced a critical temporary stability risk: lateral-torsional buckling of unbraced single beams under wet concrete, with utilisation factors exceeding 200 %. Temporary restraints were ultimately provided, but the design and check programme was compressed and most deck reinforcement had already been fixed, restricting installation options. The Expert Panel emphasised the role of the Temporary Works Coordinator, clear communication of sequence changes, and explicit treatment of temporary conditions. Network Rail has since published B&S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025 on consideration of temporary conditions.

body.h: Control expectations under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015
body.p: Temporary platforms, propping schemes that rely on existing fabric, and temporary conditions of permanent works are temporary works. They belong on the Temporary Works Register. They require competent Temporary Works Coordinator oversight, design or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity, verification of the existing structure where it forms part of the load path, and formal change control when sequence or method alters temporary stability. CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase so that work is carried out without risks to health or safety so far as is reasonably practicable, and to ensure that the stability of any structure (including temporary ones) is not compromised. BS 5975-1:2024 supplies the procedural framework that turns those duties into a live register, hold points and competent inspection. Verbal assurances, paper systems that are not implemented, and the assumption that “it is only temporary” do not discharge the duties.

posts.title: Unsupported trench, spoil at the edge, fatal burial: Banstead sentencing underlines excavation as temporary works
posts.excerpt: On 9 September 2026 the Old Bailey sentenced two firms and a contracts manager after a labourer was buried in an unsupported 10 ft trench in Banstead in 2020. No trench support, spoil piled next to the excavation, and basic precautions absent. Excavations remain temporary works and must sit on the Temporary Works Register under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM.
posts.linkedinReady:
An excavation is temporary works. If the sides are unsupported and spoil sits at the edge, the risk is not theoretical — it is the same failure mode that has killed workers for decades.

On 9 September 2026 the Old Bailey sentenced two companies and a contracts manager after the death of labourer Gheorghita Arsene, 33, in Banstead, Surrey, on 24 June 2020. He was working in an approximately 10 ft deep trench to replace a damaged pipe when a wall collapsed, burying him under tonnes of soil. Emergency services could not free him in time.

Court findings and HSE evidence showed:
• the trench had no structural support
• excavated spoil had been deposited immediately adjacent to the edge, adding surcharge
• basic, well-known precautions for excavation work were not in place

Principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited (now in liquidation) was fined £500,000. Groundworks subcontractor T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 plus £40,000 costs. Contracts manager Anthony O’Connor received a 10-month suspended sentence and unpaid work. The judge noted cost-cutting at the expense of safety and systems that existed on paper but were not implemented.

This is not a new lesson. HSE and CROSS material repeatedly show that unsupported excavations, inadequate temporary support, and uncontrolled surcharge from spoil remain recurring causes of collapse and serious injury. Under CDM 2015 the principal contractor must plan, manage and monitor the construction phase so that work is carried out without risks to health or safety so far as is reasonably practicable, and must ensure the stability of any structure (including temporary ones) is not compromised. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the management procedures that turn those duties into a live Temporary Works Register, competent Temporary Works Coordinator oversight, design or accepted standard solutions, and verified installation before people enter the excavation.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators:

• Treat every excavation that requires support, or that could affect adjacent structures or people, as an item on the Temporary Works Register.
• Do not dig until the support system (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity) has been designed or selected, checked to the appropriate category, and permitted.
• Keep spoil, plant and materials outside the zone of influence; surcharge is a design load.
• Ensure the person authorising entry or completing inspections is competent for that class of temporary works.
• Close the relevant hold points before operatives enter the trench.

body.p: On 24 June 2020 at a site on Park Road, Banstead, Surrey, where an old care home was being demolished for a new purpose-built facility, labourer Gheorghita Arsene (known as Geo), 33, was working in an approximately 10 ft (3 m) deep trench to replace a damaged pipe. He was clearing soil with hand tools when, without warning, at least one trench wall collapsed. He was buried under approximately two tonnes of soil. Colleagues and emergency services attempted rescue but could not free him in time; he was pronounced dead at the scene. The incident was investigated by the Health and Safety Executive.

body.h: What the court and HSE found
body.p: Health and safety inspectors established that the trench had no structural supports and that excavated spoil had been deposited unsafely close to the edge, increasing the risk of collapse. Basic precautions known to protect workers from the well-recognised risks of excavation work were absent. After a three-month trial at the Old Bailey, principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited and groundworks subcontractor T Vaughan Limited were found guilty of failing to discharge their duties under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Contracts manager Anthony O’Connor pleaded guilty to the same charge.

Judge Judy Khan KC sentenced Appledorn Developments Limited (by then in liquidation) to a £500,000 fine, stating there had been cost-cutting at the expense of safety and a desire to get the works done quickly and cheaply. T Vaughan Limited was fined £650,000 plus £40,000 costs; the judge noted that systems were in place on paper but had not been sufficiently adhered to or implemented, and allowed six years to pay. Anthony O’Connor, 42, of Romford, was sentenced to 10 months’ custody suspended for 18 months and 150 hours’ unpaid work; the judge found he had actual foresight of the risk of harm. An HSE spokesperson described the death as both horrifying and preventable.

body.h: Control lessons under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM
body.p: An unsupported excavation with surcharge from spoil at the crest is a classic temporary works failure mode. Excavations that require support, or that could affect the stability of adjacent ground, structures or people, belong on the Temporary Works Register. They require competent Temporary Works Coordinator oversight, design or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity, installation verification, and a closed permit or hold point before people enter. CDM 2015 places duties on the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor, and to ensure structural stability is not compromised. BS 5975-1:2024 provides the procedural framework. Verbal assurances, paper systems that are not implemented, and the assumption that “it will be fine for a short dig” do not discharge those duties. The same pattern appears in other recent HSE cases and CROSS reports involving platforms, props and masonry: temporary works treated as informal site kit rather than structures subject to formal control.

posts.title: Props removed without coordination and ad-hoc masonry bracing: two recurring temporary works failures
posts.excerpt: CROSS continues to receive reports of temporary works being altered or improvised on site without design, without Temporary Works Coordinator involvement, and without formal change control. A raking strut removed because it obstructed a pour, and timber bracing fixed to masonry walls without calculation, both illustrate the same gap: temporary stability treated as informal site kit rather than a managed system under BS 5975-1:2024.
posts.linkedinReady:
A temporary works scheme is not complete until the last prop is struck under controlled conditions. Removing one element because it is in the way, or improvising timber bracing on a partially built masonry wall, is still a design change — and design changes need coordination.

Two recent CROSS reports make the point clearly for contractors and Temporary Works Coordinators.

In CROSS Report 1388 a retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was holding a slope until a transfer slab could be built. One strut obstructed the contractor’s work on the slab, so it was removed. The result was an unsafe section of temporary works. The resident engineer had to instruct remedial works and insist that the slab be completed and the wall stabilised before any further controlled removal. The Expert Panel’s message was unambiguous: any proposed change to the design — authorised or otherwise — must be agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor; the Temporary Works Coordinator should be consulted; and on complex sites daily coordination meetings exist precisely to surface these sequencing conflicts before operatives take matters into their own hands.

In CROSS Report 1525 a reporter raised continuing concern about ad-hoc timber bracing systems used to support masonry walls during construction. These arrangements often lack design, calculations or competent oversight. The reporter had personal experience of a life-changing injury from a masonry wall collapse. The Expert Panel noted that partially completed masonry walls remain vulnerable to overturning from modest wind, impact or construction loads, and that improvised bracing can give a false sense of security while introducing unassessed failure modes. Temporary stability of masonry must be identified as temporary works, managed under BS 5975 procedures, and supported by proven or designed systems rather than site improvisation.

Both cases sit inside the same control framework that contractors already operate under CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024:

• Treat every temporary support — prop, strut, bracing, crash deck or working platform — as an item on the Temporary Works Register.
• Do not remove, modify or load any temporary works element without the Temporary Works Coordinator’s knowledge and a documented change or permit process.
• Require design (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity) before installation of temporary restraint to masonry or other free-standing elements.
• Use daily coordination and task planning to surface spatial conflicts early so that alternative sequences or temporary works redesigns can be agreed before work is forced into an unsafe condition.
• Competence matters: the person authorising a change or completing an inspection must be competent for that class of temporary works.

body.h: CROSS 1388 — temporary works strut removed prematurely
body.p: A resident engineer reported a substantial building project where a retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was containing a slope until a transfer slab could be constructed. One of the raking struts was obstructing the contractor’s work on the slab and was removed, leaving an unsafe section of temporary works. The reporter instructed remedial works and required the transfer slab to be completed and the pipe-pile wall stabilised before any further controlled removal of props. CROSS published the report (ID 1388) on 26 August 2025.

body.h: Expert Panel comments on change control
body.p: The Expert Panel observed that numerous failures have resulted from changes — authorised or otherwise — to both temporary and permanent works, often with unforeseen consequences. Any proposed change should be agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor. Where a Temporary Works Coordinator is appointed, they should be consulted so that an alternative solution can be coordinated. The contractor remains responsible for the temporary works; if progress is obstructed, the reason should be understood and the deviation communicated through the temporary works procedure rather than resolved by unilateral removal. Daily coordination meetings and detailed spatial task planning are practical tools for identifying such conflicts before operatives act.

body.h: CROSS 1525 — ad-hoc temporary bracing of masonry walls
body.p: A reporter raised concern about the continued use of ad-hoc timber bracing systems supporting masonry walls during construction. These systems frequently lack proper temporary works design, calculations or oversight, leaving structures unstable and workers exposed to serious risk. The reporter had suffered a life-changing injury from a preventable masonry wall collapse. CROSS published the report (ID 1525) on 13 May 2026. The Expert Panel confirmed that partially completed masonry walls remain vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads (wind, impact or construction activity) and that improvised bracing can provide a false sense of security while remaining unassessed.

body.h: Control expectations under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM
body.p: Temporary stability of masonry and the controlled removal or modification of props and struts are temporary works. They belong on the Temporary Works Register, require competent Temporary Works Coordinator oversight, and must not be altered by informal site decision. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the management procedures; CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase so that it is carried out without risks to health or safety so far as is reasonably practicable, and to ensure that the stability of any structure is not compromised. Design (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity), formal change control, and competent inspection close the hold points that prevent these recurring failures.

posts.title: No design, no calculated load, incompetent inspection: the Paxton House platform collapse
posts.excerpt: HSE’s June 2026 prosecution of the Paxton House temporary platform collapse underlines a recurring control failure: temporary structures used without design, without a calculated safe load, and inspected by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM require the opposite — a live register, competent oversight and verified capacity before use.

• no calculation of a safe loading level
• an inspection form completed by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator

body.p: A reporter was asked to advise on temporary works to allow removal of a defective reinforced concrete column at the base of a multi-storey block of flats, to be replaced by a new steel column. Estimated characteristic load over 1,165 kN; design load around 1,590 kN. Heavy-duty props were proposed to support beams and slab either side of the column. The prop designer had not checked the existing structure.

The proposed props could handle the forces. The existing beams and slabs were insufficient to transfer the loads, with a risk of failure in bending and shear. The column above would have continued to load the system. The reporter identified this through opening-up works, designed a more complex temporary works system and prepared a method statement. CROSS comments that this indicates a failure of the temporary works procedure — no Temporary Works Coordinator or checking engineer appointed on a significant structure.

ul: Always verify the full load path when introducing temporary supports — including existing beams, slabs, walls and foundations that will carry redistributed load.
Do not design props in isolation. Adequacy of the proprietary unit is not adequacy of the scheme.
Design briefs must require assessment of the existing structure where loads will be transferred.
Contractors and TWCs must ensure propping schemes are coordinated, checked and approved before installation.
Refurbishment creates complex temporary load cases. Each stage — permanent, temporary, back to permanent — must be planned.

body.h: How we would treat this on a live project
body.p: Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure. A column replacement under an occupied multi-storey frame is high-consequence, unusual load path, and incomplete permanent works stability. That combination typically needs a robust brief, competent design, independent check and hold points for opening-up, prop load, and column removal. Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

posts.title: ICE: temporary works are still hidden in plain sight
posts.excerpt: The Institution of Civil Engineers’ 12 May 2026 explainer is a useful plain-English reminder for clients and site teams: falsework, formwork, platforms, hoardings and sequence are engineering, not background noise. BS 5975 exists because people died getting this wrong.
posts.linkedinReady:
ICE’s May 2026 explainer is worth sending to every client who still thinks temporary works is ‘just scaffolding’.

Falsework, formwork, working platforms, hoardings, crane bases, sequence — all engineering. The TWC’s job is appointments, register, design brief, design check, permit and hold-point inspection.

We have that procedure because of collapses in the 1950s–70s, including Loddon Viaduct (1972), the Bragg Report (1975) and BS 5975 (first published 1982; split in 2024 into management and falsework design).

If your project cannot show those five steps, you do not have control. You have hope.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#ICE #BS5975 #TemporaryWorks

body.p: On 12 May 2026 ICE published a public-facing guide to temporary works: engineering solutions used to support, protect, provide or test elements while the permanent works are built. Examples include falsework, formwork, scaffolding, working platforms with edge protection, hoardings, hoists and site services. Temporary works also include the sequence of the permanent works so the structure does not become unstable mid-construction.

ul: Appointments — named people and organisations, including the Temporary Works Coordinator.
Register — a live record of items, not a spreadsheet started at tender and never updated.
Design brief — risks, constraints, loads and what ‘done’ looks like.
Design and check — including the TWC’s confirmation that the check is appropriate.
Permit and hold points — inspected on site before load, use, alteration or strike.

body.p: ICE recaps the line from major accidents in the 1950s–70s, including the Loddon Viaduct collapse in 1972, through the Bragg Report (1975) to BS 5975 (first published 1982). The 2024 revision split the standard: BS 5975-1 for management procedures and BS 5975-2 for falsework design. That split is useful — but only if both parts are actually used. A design to Part 2 without Part 1 control is a drawing without a permit.

body.h: Use it as a toolbox talk
body.p: This explainer is written for a wide audience. That makes it a good handout for clients, supervisors and graduates. Pair it with a site example from your own register: one item, one brief, one check, one permit, one inspection. Then ask: which of our live items cannot show all five?
